title: Penn State men’s hockey stays in win column, sweeps Canisius
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
In the first of the two-game series Friday night, Penn State stood arm-in-arm along the blue line and joined the Roar Zone in the Alma Mater for the first time this season, after breaking its 0-4 start by downing Canisius 5-1.

History repeated itself Saturday, and the Nittany Lions completed the series sweep with a 3-2 overtime win over the Golden Griffins.

“We didn’t have our best start, but I think this weekend, kind of figuring out our game…we knew all along that we’re going to be a competitive team,” freshman goaltender Ryder Fetterolf said. “Getting the first sweep feels great, and it’s kind of just giving us a small taste of what we got ahead.”

The blue and white seemed to carry its momentum over from the previous victory and came out strong in its rematch against Canisius.

Senior defenseman Casey Aman came inches from putting Penn State on the board after his shot trickled past goaltender Jack Lisson. Still, the puck was kicked away by a Canisius defender just before it crossed the goal line.

The physicality also picked back up right where it left off, and the Nittany Lions were given the game’s first power play after defenseman Carter Patterson was called for cross-checking about halfway through the period.

Despite a few good chances, the blue and white couldn’t get anything through.

Senior defenseman Mac Gadowsky was the one to finally break the ice for the Nittany Lions with just under four minutes left in the period.

After receiving a pass out by the blue line with no one around, Mac Gadowsky fired a long-range shot that found its way through traffic and into the back of the net.

With under two minutes to play, senior captain Dane Dowiak was called for tripping, sending the Nittany Lions into the first intermission with a one-goal lead, but about 30 seconds of the penalty to kill off.

The blue and white successfully returned to 5-on-5 play to begin the second period, but much of the remaining middle frame didn’t go its way.

The Golden Griffins had their best chance of the night when senior forward Ethan Wolthers went unseen behind two Penn State defenders and was left open on a breakaway. Fetterolf — who had been extremely solid for the Nittany Lions so far — made the save to keep the team ahead, however.

“I thought (Fetterolf) was really good when he needed to be, and you can see what a battler he is,” Guy Gadowsky said.

The blue and white continued to hold onto its lead, although struggling to regain its momentum from the first period. With under five minutes to play in the period, Canisius finally got on the board after sophomore forward David Elmy picked up a blocked shot and fired it past Fetterolf.

Another solid save by Fetterolf a few minutes later turned into some shoving after the whistle, and matching roughing penalties ensued on Canisius’s Joe Messina and Penn State’s Shea Van Olm.

It took less than 10 seconds for the Golden Griffins to capitalize on the 4-on-4 opportunity when senior forward Rhys Chiddenton’s shot found the back of the net and sent his team into the second intermission with their first lead of the night.

Penn State’s third period looked to be off to a rocky start when defenseman Nick Fascia was called for tripping just three minutes in. Still, the penalty was negated about 30 seconds later when Canisius’ Hunter Price went to the box, also for tripping.

Neither team capitalized on its man-up opportunities, but less than a minute after returning to equal strength, the blue and white evened the score once again. Sophomore Justin Poirier sent a one-timer from the left circle off the crossbar and into the net to tie the game with about 15 minutes still to play.

With a tie game and only a minute to play, former Nittany Lion turned Canisius defenseman Jason Gallucci was given a delay-of-game penalty.

Despite the late-game man-advantage, 60 minutes wasn’t enough to decide a winner, and Pegula Ice Arena headed to overtime.

It was a short-lived overtime, and defenseman Jackson Smith called game just 15 seconds in, after Fetterolf made a diving save that sent Smith and Poirier on a 2-on-1 the other way. Smith ripped a shot to the top corner of Canisius’ goal and sealed Penn State’s 3-2 victory.

“Great save by (Fetterolf), that was huge, and then a little rebound and he got another save,” Smith said. “I kind of stretched the zone a bit and took a chance. I got a nice pass from (Poirier) and took my shot.”

Up Next

Penn State is back on the road to open Big Ten play against Minnesota, with puck drop scheduled for 8 p.m. Friday at 3M Arena at Mariucci.

title: 3-star RB Jordan Hall commits to Penn State
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has added another piece to its 2027 class.

The Nittany Lions earned a commitment from 3-star running back Jordan Hall, he announced Saturday.

The Cincinnati native was previously committed to Miami Ohio, but decommitted in August. He received offers from hometown Ohio State on Sept. 5 and Missouri on Sept. 16, but visited Happy Valley for the White Out game and wound up committing to the Nittany Lions two weeks later.

The Princeton High School star is the No. 32 player from Ohio and No. 60 running back in his class, according to 247Sports composite.

The Nittany Lions now have two running back commits, with Hall joining 3-star Chukwuma Odoh.

Matt Campbell visited Hall at his high school game on Friday night, making one final push to add him to his first full recruiting class at Penn State.

title: No. 6 Penn State women's hockey battles St. Lawrence into overtime, winning with a last-minute goal
author: Henry Bustin | For The Collegian
description:
Following a 3-1 victory against St. Lawrence University’s Saints on Friday evening, No. 6 Penn State women’s hockey led a close match against the Saints for the second day, going into overtime and clinching a last-minute goal to win 2-1.

First period

The period began with intense back-and-forth pressure between the Saints and the Nittany Lions, creating an exciting atmosphere in Appleton Arena.

St. Lawrence stopped an attempted goal from the blue and white. Soon after, freshman goalie Morgan Stickney skillfully deflected a goal and then blocked another attempt by St. Lawrence’s Riley Reeves.

As the teams continued to battle, Nittany Lions’ freshman Kylie Amelkovich attempted a high shot, which St. Lawrence blocked.

A power play began soon after, and on the breakout, Penn State led the puck up the ice, but its hustle was cut short as St. Lawrence launched it upward.

With under 10 minutes left in the quarter, St. Lawrence applied pressure during a 4-on-4 power play against the blue and white, with a quick shot that Stickney deflected yet again.

Soon afterward, a penalty was called on Penn State during a power play with 1:02 left, directly after Stickney deflected a goal.

As St. Lawrence’s Brooke Mulvihill tried to advance the puck toward Penn State’s net, the blue and white’s junior forward McKenna Walsh disrupted her attempt and sent it flying to St. Lawrence’s side so Penn State could keep applying pressure.

With even strength between the teams and six minutes remaining in the period, St. Lawrence launched several attempts on Penn State, which Stickney continued to deflect away.

With 2:51 remaining in the quarter, 10 shots had been attempted, six from the Nittany Lions and four from the Saints; none entered the net.

As 14.4 seconds remained in the quarter, St. Lawrence nearly scored a goal, but Stickney deflected it away.

Second period

The period kicked off with St. Lawrence applying pressure in the first minute, with Stickney blocking a goal attempt.

The Nittany Lions drove the puck up and launched it at the net, which the Saints’ goalie, Kassidy Lawrence, just managed to save.

As St. Lawrence tried to advance towards Penn State’s goal, blue and white sophomore defender Sophie Morrow stole the puck from the Saints and drove it away from Penn State’s crease, but it was soon returned to the Nittany Lions’ side.

With 15 minutes remaining, two shot attempts were made on Penn State, but Stickney skillfully blocked them both. Stickney had nine blocks with 10 minutes remaining in the period, displaying her superior goalie skills as well as those of Penn State’s defense.

The two teams continued with goal attempts, and Amelkovich nearly scored but wasn’t successful.

Soon after, with around 8:30 remaining in the period, a backhand assist to St. Lawrence first-year Sonia Mehta allowed her to score a first-career goal on the Nittany Lions, granting the Saints a 1-0 lead.

The teams continued to battle it out, with Stickney rejecting numerous attempts made by the Saints.

A buzzer-beater shot was launched by the Nittany Lions but did not go through. The period ended with the Saints still ahead 1-0, making the final frame vital for Penn State to make a comeback.

Third period

The period started with the Nittany Lions in possession of the puck. They were looking to remove the deficit that the Saints had been banking on from the previous two periods.

With 18:27 in the period, a penalty was called on Penn State for a hugging call, granting the Saints a Power Play.

St. Lawrence made a few shot attempts during the power play, which were blocked by Stickney.

With 14:08 remaining in the period, Nittany Lions’ freshman defender Megan Hosman launched a successful slap shot goal in the midst of a power play, tying the game 1-1, boosting the morale of the blue and white.

Soon after, with 12:40 remaining, a penalty was called on the Nittany Lions, resulting in a power play for the Saints. They applied heavy pressure in Penn State’s crease, but defensive players Hosman and Morrow, combined with the goalkeeping of Stickney, prevented any successful goals.

The Nittany Lions and the Saints continued the game with several power plays after penalties were called, most notably on Abby Stonehouse for roughing with around 11 minutes remaining. This allowed multiple opportunities for the Saints to make goal attempts, with several coming from Mulvihill, Hehl, and Haslam, but none were successful as Stickney continued to deflect.

The Nittany Lions retaliated with shots of their own but also were unable to score on the Saints.

The period ended tied 1-1, prompting the two teams to go into overtime.

Overtime

Overtime began with Penn State’s Mikah Keller winning the faceoff. Several shot attempts were made by Amelkovich, Danica Maynard and Grace Outwater, but none made contact with the net.

The two teams went back and forth with strategic plays like drop passes and slap shots, but it appeared they were at a near-stalemate until, with 31.1 seconds remaining in the period, Outwater scored, securing the Nittany Lions' series sweep over the Saints.

Up Next

Next Friday, the Nittany Lions take on the RIT Tigers at the Gene Polisseni Center, with puck drop slated for 6 p.m.

title: Penn State men’s hockey gets first win of the season behind captain’s multi-goal effort
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State captain Dane Dowiak sat at the podium Tuesday night after the team’s 5-2 loss to Robert Morris and took ownership of its 0-4 start to the season.

“I know I got to be better. I got to lead this team right. I haven’t done that yet,” Dowiak said after the loss. “So we’re going to do a little bit of self-reflection, take a look in the mirror and turn this thing around.”

Dowiak was true to his word and led the Nittany Lions to their first win of the season, downing Canisius 5-1 behind his own two-goal performance.

“(Dowiak) played a really excellent team game,” coach Guy Gadowsky said. “Often when guys do that, they get rewarded.”

The senior forward’s first tally provided an early spark to the blue and white’s momentum. Less than three minutes into play, freshman forward Justin Larose sent a slot pass to Dowiak from behind the net, and his shot beat goaltender Jack Lisson.

Penn State has struggled with maintaining leads this season, so when sophomore defenseman Jackson Smith was called for interference shortly after the goal, it needed a crucial penalty kill.

After letting up only one shot, the Nittany Lions successfully returned to 5-on-5 play.

Nothing came of the rest of the period, but the blue and white entered the first intermission with a one-goal lead and holding an 11-5 edge in shots.

Penn State was back on its heels when, under two minutes into the middle frame, Canisius freshman Ben Brunelle notched his first collegiate goal after picking the corner on Josh Fleming’s net and equalizing the score.

The Nittany Lions only spent the next two minutes tied at one-a-piece before freshman Andrew Kuzma also registered his first collegiate goal and pulled the Nittany Lions back ahead.

After Smith’s initial shot was blocked, freshman forward Kale Dach picked up the loose puck and found Kuzma down low before firing it into the back of the net.

The physicality between the two non-conference opponents started to ramp up as the second period played on, and two more penalties, this time on the Golden Griffins, were called.

Nothing came for the Nittany Lions on the first power play, but Dowiak capitalized during his team’s second man-advantage of the period. The captain was waiting down low, and once he received a pass from sophomore forward Lev Katzin, Dowiak threw the puck on net, which was redirected off a skate and in.

“(Dowiak) made several excellent changes, including on the power play,” Gadowsky said. “He back-checked extremely hard. He was covering up for people.”

The third period was much of the same, with the blue and white maintaining a majority of puck possession.

The score held until late in the final frame, when Kuzma tallied an empty-net goal to join Dowiak with a multi-goal game.

The Nittany Lions still had one more goal to send the Golden Griffins home with, however, after a shorthanded opportunity led to Smith firing the puck off the crossbar and in with just five seconds to play, and sealing the team’s first win of the season, 5-1.

“We all knew after the (Robert Morris) game that ‘it’s really time now,’” Smith said. “It’s pretty cool if we can come back from this tough start, but now we have a chance to have a pretty cool story.”

title: Penn State women's soccer's Aubrey Kulpa, Paige Pasinski named TDS Midseason Top 100 players
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s Aubrey Kulpa and Paige Pasinski have been named to Top Drawer Soccer’s Midseason Top 100 following their respective performances throughout the year.

Freshman midfielder Pasinski has found herself earning regular starting assignments and heavy minutes in conference play, tallying five points via two goals and one assist.

The Phoenix native has showcased herself to be an offensive facilitator on the pitch, earning her the 47th spot out of 100.

Kulpa, the Cromwell, Connecticut, native, is a well-known force for the Nittany Lions. The junior forward is leading the blue and white with 18 points via seven goals and four assists, proving dominance over any competitor time and time again.

title: Homecourt helps propel No. 16 Penn State women's volleyball to win over No. 10 Oregon
author: Matthew Bakken | For The Collegian
description:
No. 16 Penn State returned home to a ruckus crowd at Rec Hall after a long West Coast trip. No. 10 Oregon had a long trip of its own, both geographically and during the game, as the Nittany Lions cruised to a 3-1 victory.

“I mean, we love playing at home. It's nice, and it was a great crowd tonight,” Penn State head coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley said postgame.

It certainly was, as Rec Hall had a booming echo throughout, with the blue and white giving the home crowd plenty to cheer about after a taxing road trip.

The Nittany Lions have had to deal with the Western powers of the Big Ten as of late, splitting a trip to Southern California last weekend.

“Mean, it's, I mean that's, you know everyone's got to do it in the league though. So you know it's it's a tough travel, but you know I think the teams that you know are focused and can you know stay the course, you know do a good job,” Schumacher-Cawley said about the contrasting travel toll for Penn State. “It was nice to see us split last weekend and you know win at home.”

Despite every Big Ten team having to deal with the effects of the long travel. It’s hard not to think that the travel had an effect on Oregon, as the Ducks came out sluggish in the first set. Conversely, Penn State with some help from the Rec Hall crowd had a noticeable edge to them.

An edge even in a 3-0 win at USC last weekend, the Nittany Lions lacked with the toll of traveling that far away. The advantage of being able to close out and finish Oregon in the fourth set might not have taken place had the game been in Eugene. As just a week ago UCLA used its home-court advantage to stun the blue and white late at night.

It’s hard not to think travel dictates how Penn State plays, as the Nittany Lions boast an impressive 10-2 mark at home compared to middling 3-2 away and 1-1 neutral court records. Those two home losses also came to two teams currently in the top-10 in Nebraska and Tennessee. Any concerns about the blue and white not being able to compete with the top teams could be squashed after defeating a top-10 Oregon tonight in a dominating fashion.

Despite the big one tonight, Schumacher-Cawley’s focus was on the future.

“You know this is the first year for the Big Ten Tournament, so putting ourselves in a great position for that,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “And you know it's nice to see us get better every match and continue to do that. We have eight more regular season matches.”

Luckily, the Nittany Lions don’t need to see the West anymore, even if it was won. Just the comforts of Happy Valley, three more home games and five short Midwestern road trips remain on the season as Penn State pushes not just for the Big Ten Tournament but the NCAA Tournament as well.

title: No. 16 Penn State women’s volleyball gets top-10 victory over No. 10 Oregon in Dig Pink match
author: Joey Bolger | For The Collegian
description:
No. 16 Penn State held its annual Dig Pink game at Rec Hall on Friday night, welcoming No. 10 Oregon in a Big Ten heavyweight clash.

Penn State won in four sets to get its first top-10 victory since Sept. 11 against then-No. 4 Stanford. Kennedy Martin led the Nittany Lions with 25 kills and got the last kill to seal the match for the Nittany Lions.

The Nittany Lions came out with two liberos in senior Jocelyn Nathan and junior Ava Falduto, an interesting move from coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley, as Nathan and Falduto have been on the court at the same time for most of this season.

“So we’re you know we’re just trying to use everyone and get the best out of them to find ways to score points and win,” Schumacher-Cawley said.

The blue and white came out firing early in the first set, taking a commanding 10-5 lead with Kendall Northern putting up three kills. Setter Alexis Stucky also shined during the first set, grabbing two kills and eight assists.

Penn State committed six service errors in the first set, allowing the Ducks to keep the slate competitive.

A thunderous swing from Martin sealed the first set for the Nittany Lions 25-17. Penn State’s offense was efficient, having a .545 hit percentage and having a perfect sideout percentage. Oregon couldn’t get anything going on offense, having a .071 hit percentage.

However, in the second set, the Ducks started to come alive, holding the lead for a majority of the set with Sjakkie Donkers and Alanah Clemente having seven kills.

Just as the momentum shifted in Oregon’s favor as the Ducks went up 19-16, Penn State responded with a 3-0 scoring run, forcing Oregon to take a timeout and regroup.

Both teams went back and forth at the end of the second set, but a kill from Donkers put the Ducks right back into the match, winning a scrappy second set 25-23 and tying the match at 1-1.

Penn State’s offense showed some flaws in the second set as its hitting percentage dipped from .545 to .333.

Backed by an electric home crowd, Penn State took an early 9-6 lead in the third set with Martin having three kills. Momentum continued to go in the Nittany Lions' direction, going up 13-8 and forcing Oregon to spend a timeout early on in the third set.

Coming out of the timeout, both teams put out an impressive rally which ended with a Penn State kill by Whitney Lauenstein, putting the home crowd on their feet.

Down 18-12, the Ducks went on a 3-0 scoring run, forcing the Nittany Lions to take a timeout. This decision paid off as Penn State grabbed the first two points coming out of the timeout.

Penn State held off the Ducks to close out a convincing third set, 25-19, thanks to a block assist by Gabrielle Nichols and Martin, which put the Nittany Lions up 2-1.

Martin played a huge role in the third set, having eight kills along with a block assist to end the set. Penn State’s offense bounced back after a defensive second set, improving its hitting percentage to .353.

The Martin show persisted in the fourth set, claiming five kills of Penn State’s eight points early on.

The Ducks’ energy never wavered as they went on a 3-0 scoring run to gain an 11-9 lead. Donkers led the offense with three kills early on to give Oregon life.

Resiliency was a main factor for Penn State all night, as every time Oregon looked to gain momentum or start to pull ahead, the blue and white found a way to fight back into the set.

“When we’re at our best, all communicating, all working as a unit, fearless,” Lauenstein said. “Going for everything, swinging away, not thinking about the next or not thinking about errors.”

Once again, both teams traded blows late in the fourth set with both sides refusing to leave Rec Hall without a major Big Ten win.

Penn State held the momentum late into the match, sealing the fourth set, 25-20.

“We’re just very unified when we’re at our best,” Nathan said.

Up Next

The Nittany Lions will make the trip to Bloomington on Sunday to take on the No. 18 Indiana Hoosiers on FS1 at 3 p.m.

MORE VOLLEYBALL COVERAGE

title: Penn State men’s hockey snaps 4-game losing streak backed by 2-goal game from captain
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State captain Dane Dowiak spun around and fell flat on his back celebrating a goal in the first period. He made sure to stay upright after potting his second.

With questions to be answered and statements to be made, the Nittany Lions penciled in their first win of the season, defeating Canisius 5-1 behind a much-needed performance by their captain.

“Great night, and very important to us too,” coach Guy Gadowsky said. “We needed that. It was absolutely a great team win. Great crowd, which helped a lot.”

Here’s how Penn State finally got into the win column Friday night, ending a four-game losing streak and delivering a monumental sigh of relief to a Nittany Lions fanbase that really needed one.

First period

So much for the slow starts. Penn State scored first for just the second time this season — both at home — thanks to a nifty pass from left wing Justin Larose.

The freshman trailed linemate Justin Poirier two minutes into the game as he swerved around a duo of Canisius defenders, into the Golden Griffins zone and behind goaltender Jack Lisson.

After Poirier lost his footing, Larose scooped up the puck and put it on captain Dane Dowiak’s tape in the slot, who lifted the puck over a sprawling Lisson and into the back of the net to give Penn State a 1-0 lead. Talk about a response from the captain after he, like Gadowsky, called the team out on Tuesday night.

“He made several excellent changes for the team,” Gadowsky said. “... He back-checked extremely hard. He was covering up for people. He played a really excellent team game, and often when guys do that, they get rewarded.”

That was all the scoring for what was a physical first frame. The Nittany Lions hit a post, had a 3-on-1 rush and a few other opportunities, but never cashed in. Canisius, on the other hand, was stymied, as Penn State dominated puck control and outshot the Golden Griffins 11-5.

Second period

Canisius came out of the locker room firing.

After controlling the first minute of the period and applying heavy pressure on Penn State, center Ben Brunelle corralled the puck at the red line before skating into the Nittany Lions’ zone.

Brunelle, while staving off defenseman Ethan Weber, fired the puck from an unusual angle, picking the top-left corner of the net and tying the game at one 1:18 into the frame.

That didn’t last for long; Penn State answered almost immediately.

Defenseman Jackson Smith wristed a shot from the point that ricocheted off Lisson, leaked into the slot and landed on the stick of center Kale Dach.

Dach, who made a last-ditch effort to reach the sliding puck, one-handed it to left wing Andrew Kuzma for an easy one-timer to retake the lead. It was Kuzma’s, who had open-heart surgery in 2024 that caused him to medically redshirt, first collegiate goal.

“Andrew Kuzma scores the first goal after everything that guy has been through was really really cool to see,” Gadowsky said. “He deserved it and his family could not have handled his situation better, and so you cheer for guys like that so much. So I give him so much credit. So great to see.”

The Nittany Lions padded their lead 10 minutes later, with Dowiak tallying his second score on the man-advantage. The senior center leisurely controlled the puck by the bottom of the right-wing circle before firing it into a cluster of skaters, where the puck deflected off a player and into the Canisius goal, extending Penn State’s advantage to 3-1.

Third period

The third period showcased less theatrics.

Canisius had two power-play opportunities, but neither team generated many high-danger chances. Nittany Lions center Kaden Pitre dinged a post, which was about the best scoring opportunity for either program.

However, Kuzma drilled an empty-netter — his second score Friday — to ice the game. Smith scored with five seconds remaining in regulation to extend Penn State's lead to 5-1.

After a low-eventful third frame, the Nittany Lions prevailed, holding onto its lead and defeating the Golden Griffins in regulation. Penn State outshot Canisius 44-24, with netminder Josh Fleming dazzling in net, posting a .957 save percentage.

Injury report

Sophomore center Luke Misa slammed hard into the boards early in the first period Friday night, hobbling off the ice with the referees' help and going immediately to the locker room. He returned in the second period.

Up Next

Penn State concludes its stretch of six consecutive non-conference contests to open the season on Saturday, as the Nittany Lions are scheduled to finish their two-game set with Canisius. Puck drop is slated for 5 p.m. ET at Pegula Ice Arena.

MORE HOCKEY COVERAGE

title: No. 6 Penn State women's hockey defeats St. Lawrence to open series on the road
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State traveled to Canton, New York, Friday evening to face St. Lawrence in a close battle that went down to the wire.

Ultimately, the Nittany Lions prevailed 3-1 over the Saints in a pivotal road game.

The result improved the blue and white to 6-3 on the young season, before closing out the series tomorrow.

First period

Penn State and St. Lawrence battled it out on the offensive end in the opening minutes of the game.

Taya MacDonald hit her shot wide in the first 10 seconds. Soon after, St. Lawrence’s Ella Nancarrow blocked Danica Maynard’s shot. \

The Nittany Lions seemed to push hard early. But the Saints would not sit back for long. Penn State goaltender Morgan Stickney kept the scoresheet clean as Abby Hehl and Brooke Mulvihill tested the freshman netminder.

At the other end, Kassidy Lawrence proved to be just as sharp, denying Grace Tullock, Ashley Kokavec, Megan Hosman, and Alanna Devlin on several chances around the net.

Then, at 6:56, St. Lawrence scored the goal that broke through Penn State’s scoreless start. With both goalies already called into action multiple times that period, the Saints capitalized on the opportunity, finding the back of the net off a Mae Severn–Rylan Haslam assist and handing the No. 7-ranked Penn State team a goal to chase down.

The Nittany Lions responded to the Saints’ goal by pressing forward, with Sydney McIntosh testing Lawrence twice in quick succession.

Penn State couldn’t break through the Saints’ tight defense, as Nancarrow blocked an attempt before another Penn State effort went wide. Penn State then got another chance to convert on the power play when Kennedy Emerson received a two-minute minor for tripping with 10:09 in the period.

The Nittany Lions tested the St. Lawrence Penalty kill with several shots. Still, the Saints were able to survive the pressure and prevent the equalizer thanks to blocks by Alex Theriean and Barbora Jurickova.

Later in the period, St. Lawrence looked to put distance between itself and Penn State. However, Stickney managed to keep her team close despite facing shots from Alexia Cote, Kendall Doiron, Kennedy Emerson, and Jaylee Mackinnon.

The blue and white never relaxed its efforts to tie the game, and the final minutes were another grueling back-and-forth battle as Grace Outwater, Kokavec, Sophie Morrow, Kylie Amelkovich and Stonehouse all created late offensive chances.

The Saints showed excellent composure in the St. Lawrence Crease and maintained the slim lead. The period ended with St. Lawrence leading 1-0, thanks to Severns’ goal at 6:56. The Nittany Lions showed plenty of offensive firepower in the first 20 minutes, but the Saints had the only goal to their name.

Second period

Penn State came out hoping to level the score in the second period, as Kylie Amelkovich shot wide four seconds after the opening faceoff.

The Saints then applied pressure themselves, as Alex Therien had a shot blocked by Taya MacDonald before Jaylee MacKinnon sent another shot wide. The Nittany Lions searched for an equalizer again, as Sydney McIntosh tested Kassidy Lawrence early in the period.

At the other end, the Saints threatened when Mae Severn tested Morgan Stickney, who made the save to keep Penn State within striking distance.

Barbora Jurickova also tested Stickney, while Sophie Morrow had a shot blocked by Therien and Abby Stonehouse tested Lawrence, but neither team found the back of the net.

The Nittany Lions made their latest offensive push when Lorelai Nelson sent a shot wide and Grace Outwater tested Lawrence twice in quick succession. Another attempt by Nicole Hall followed, but Lawrence continued to make saves in the St. Lawrence crease.

The Saints reacted with chances from Rylan Haslam and Jurickova, but Stickney held firm to keep the deficit at one.

As the period progressed, St. Lawrence increased its offensive pressure. Jurickova tested Stickney again, while Ella Nancarrow had Hall block an attempt. Haslam added two more shots, but Stickney saved both to keep Penn State in the game.

The Nittany Lions searched for that tying goal again, but the Saints’ defense repeatedly denied them.

Therien blocked Outwater's attempt, while Riley Reeves blocked Morrow’s shot. Following a media timeout, McKenna Walsh tested Lawrence twice, but the St. Lawrence goalkeeper saved both attempts.

Penn State continued to apply pressure through the middle of the period.

Nicole Hall sent a shot wide before Sofia Ismael tested Lawrence, and then Abby Stonehouse sent an attempt wide. Kennedy Emerson blocked another Ismael shot as Morrow searched for an opening in the Saints’ defense.

In the later stages of the period, the Nittany Lions continued to fire.

Sonia Mehta blocked Danica Maynard’s effort before Brooke Mulvihill sent a shot wide for St. Lawrence. Amelkovich and Maynard also had chances, but their attempts went wide, while Therien produced another crucial block to keep the Saints ahead.

Penn State never gave up in the final minutes.

Lorelai Nelson and Grace Outwater tested Lawrence, while Outwater and Grace Tullock both sent shots wide as the Nittany Lions searched for a goal. St. Lawrence also created late chances through Kennedy Emerson and Jaylee MacKinnon, but both shots went wide.

At the horn, St. Lawrence led 1–0 going into the third period. Penn State created several scoring chances in the middle frame, but the Saints’ defense continued to hold the Nittany Lions off the scoreboard.

Penn State needed to build on its offensive pressure with 20 minutes left to play to keep its comeback hopes alive.

Third period

Penn State came into the third period looking to erase its one-goal deficit, but St. Lawrence got going early. Abby Hehl, Alex Therien and Kendall Doiron each tested Morgan Stickney in the opening minutes, but the Penn State goaltender kept the Saints from extending their lead.

The Nittany Lions replied with chances of their own, as Kylie Amelkovich sent a shot wide before Lorelai Nelson and Taya MacDonald tested Kassidy Lawrence in the St. Lawrence crease.

Penn State continued to search for an equalizer as Hehl blocked Sophie Morrow's shot before Nicole Hall sent an attempt wide. Then, Grace Outwater tested Lawrence, but the Saints’ goaltender continued to turn away the Nittany Lions’ chances.

At the other end, St. Lawrence looked to increase its lead, but Rylan Haslam sent a shot wide and Alexia Côté had an attempt blocked by Nelson. Barbora Jurickova also tested Stickney, but Danica Maynard made two crucial blocks to keep the deficit at one.

Still, the Nittany Lions searched for a breakthrough as Outwater tested Lawrence and Grace Tullock had an attempt blocked by Lilien Benakova. St. Lawrence created chances through Jaylee MacKinnon and Kennedy Emerson, but both shots went wide.

Penn State kept pressing, with Sofia Ismael and McKenna Walsh testing Lawrence, but the St. Lawrence goaltender kept the narrow lead intact.

Then, at 11:53, Penn State broke through. After continuing to apply pressure in the offensive zone, Abby Stonehouse found the back of the net, with Kylie Amelkovich providing the assist. The goal tied the game at 1–1 and gave the Nittany Lions new life as they looked to complete the comeback.

With momentum shifting, Penn State continued to attack. Alanna Devlin and Lorelai Nelson both sent shots wide, but the Nittany Lions kept pushing forward. St. Lawrence then took a major hit when Alex Therien received a five-minute major penalty for hitting from behind at 13:47.

Penn State was awarded a power play, giving the Nittany Lions a significant opportunity to take the lead.

The Nittany Lions took advantage. At 14:22, Stonehouse scored her second goal of the period, with Sofia Ismael providing the assist to put Penn State ahead 2–1. The goal gave the Nittany Lions their first lead of the game and put the Saints under further pressure to respond.

Penn State maintained its offensive momentum, keeping St. Lawrence under pressure and creating more chances. A shot from Grace Outwater went wide before Stonehouse sent another attempt off target.

The Nittany Lions continued to attack, and at 17:37, Outwater found the back of the net, with Mikah Keller providing the assist. The goal extended Penn State’s lead to 3–1 and put the Nittany Lions firmly in control.

St. Lawrence looked to respond in the closing minutes, but Stickney remained composed in goal, making a save on Doiron’s late attempt. Penn State also continued to battle for possession, while Benakova blocked shots from Sophie Morrow and Danica Maynard.

When the final horn sounded, Penn State had completed an impressive third-period comeback, scoring three unanswered goals to defeat St. Lawrence 3–1. After trailing 1–0 through the first two periods, the Nittany Lions found their breakthrough through Stonehouse, who scored twice, before Outwater added the insurance goal.

With strong goaltending from Stickney and a third-period offensive surge, Penn State turned a one-goal deficit into a two-goal victory.

Up next

The blue and white continue against the Saints tomorrow to close out its series at 3 p.m.

title: No. 19 Penn State field hockey defeats No. 13 Indiana in narrow clash, extends win streak to 8
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
Following Penn State’s back-to-back victories over Ohio State and Michigan this past weekend, the Nittany Lions faced the Indiana Hoosiers in Bloomington on Friday in their first of three remaining games of the 2026 regular season.

Coming into this matchup, the blue and white were in the midst of a seven-game winning streak dating back to their win over the Bucknell Bison on September 28.

After a defensive-oriented contest with the Hoosiers, Penn State beat Indiana 1-0 in regulation to continue that stretch.

Both the Nittany Lions and the Hoosiers entered the game tied for 3rd place in the Big Ten standings behind the Maryland Terrapins and Northwestern Wildcats.

Penn State entered Bloomington on a 7-game winning streak.

The opening minutes of the first quarter were slow and deliberate, as both offenses tried to establish early momentum.

The Nittany Lions were able to keep Indiana out of their own defensive circle as the physicality increased.

At the eight-minute mark of the first quarter, neither team had given up a penalty corner.

Junior goalkeeper Aby Deverka’s first save came with just under 7 minutes remaining in the first, and the score remained 0-0.

Indiana regained momentum with a free hit at the three-minute mark of the opening period, but it didn't lead to a scoring chance for the Hoosiers.

The first 15 minutes of action ended with neither team able to score or earn a single penalty corner.

The second quarter began with the first penalty corner of the game being awarded to Indiana with 13 minutes remaining.

Penn State’s defense held strong and kept the Hoosiers from taking any shot on target.

The next few minutes were back and forth, with each team unable to keep possession for more than a minute at a time.

Redshirt freshman Hope Russo’s shot with 9 minutes left in the first half fell just short, and the score remained 0-0.

Both Indiana and Penn State were locked in a defense-minded contest as the second quarter rolled on.

Indiana’s second penalty corner came with 1:11 remaining in the first half. Deverka’s block kept the score even for the Nittany Lions.

The score remained 0-0 at the halftime break, despite both sides being able to generate scoring opportunities more consistently in the second quarter.

Penn State began the third quarter with a free hit as the Nittany Lions looked to build an early offensive advantage.

Despite an early Indiana power play to start the second half, the blue and white held firm despite being down a player.

Penn State’s fast break chance with just over 8 minutes remaining in the 3rd was quickly stopped by the Hoosier backline.

At the midway point of the 3rd, the Nittany Lions had zero penalty corners, and Indiana had just two.

Indiana’s goal by senior forward Theresa Ricci with 4 minutes remaining in the 3rd was called back after a post-play review, and the score stayed at 0-0.

Penn State’s first penalty corner opportunity came with just 2.2 seconds left in the 3rd quarter. The Nittany Lions were able to capture the buzzer-beating goal to take a 1-0 lead from a shot by sophomore forward Lara Pyle.

The intensity of both teams increased at to start of the fourth quarter as Penn State worked to defend its narrow lead while the Hoosiers looked to tie it up.

Indiana earned its 3rd penalty corner chance with 10:51 remaining in regulation. Upon review, the call on the field stood firm. The Nittany Lion defensive line blocked all three shots, and the lead remained at one goal.

Indiana pulled its goalkeeper, junior Sadie Canelii, to add an extra offensive player in an attempt to score the equalizer with just under 6 minutes remaining in regulation.

After a hectic final two minutes of play, the Nittany Lions earned a penalty corner with an open net with 7.8 seconds remaining.

Penn State chose to run the clock out and seal the win in Bloomington.

Up next

The Nittany Lions will now prepare to face the Iowa Hawkeyes in Iowa City on Sunday at noon.

title: Penn State basketball shoots into the season with ‘Ball at East Hall’
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Penn State men’s and women’s basketball teams joined forces to usher in the season with their annual “Ball at East Hall” event.

Students flooded the outdoor basketball court emblazoned with the Nittany Lion head logo to meet the teams through live introductions, shooting contests and performances by the Lionettes and cheerleaders.

One attendee, Jake Dotzel, enjoyed the event and is still looking forward to basketball’s return to Happy Valley after a few tumultuous seasons.

“It was a great experience,” Dotzel, a first-year from Berwyn, Pennsylvania, said. “All the fellas came down, watched, got excited for Penn State men’s and women’s basketball. I love Penn State, I’m excited for the basketball season, and I’ve had the date on my calendar to buy tickets pinned for about a month now.”

Ball at East Hall drummed up excitement for the season the night before the men’s team’s season tickets went on sale, a reality that pleased Connor Litchfield.

“I think it’s gonna be awesome; it’s gonna be electric,” the first-year Bloomsburg, Pennsylvania, native, said. “Tickets go on sale tomorrow, so it’s good to see some support right before ticket sales.”

The emcee for the evening, Joe Putnam, kicked off the festivities by welcoming the Lady Lions, who danced through a tunnel of students while tossing out T-shirts.

Coach Tanisha Wright followed her team out and rallied the crowd by appealing to the love for Penn State that she shares. Wright is a 2005 Penn State graduate now bent on revitalizing a program that went undefeated at home twice in her playing days.

“You represent the university in a special way,” Wright said. “You guys are Penn Staters, right? You love this place. We know we support each other. Everything we do, we do it together.”

After the men’s team sauntered through the tunnel and blessed the crowd with more T-shirts, Mike Rhoades took the stage. Rhoades called on students to get to the Bryce Jordan Center early in the season to support both teams.

The fourth-year coach encouraged the Legion of Blue, Penn State’s student section, to talk to both referees and opponents early and often, and returned to a refrain that continues to gain popularity on campus: “Sweat with us.”

The Lionettes briefly hopped into the spotlight, then it was competition time.

Each team trotted out three players to compete with students in a skills competition. Anthony Grob won the event among students and earned free student season tickets.

“It was great,” the second-year from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, said. “It was great to interact with the players, have a bunch of students out just getting hyped for the season.”

The festivities rolled right along into a game of knockout. The student-athletes dominated, and Reggie Grodin won a drawn-out battle. Grodin, the redshirt freshman, dueled the Lady Lions’ Enjulina Gonzalez for the crown after the pair eliminated all other challengers.

After crowning the student champions, Putnam thanked the crowd and bade the teams good luck. Noah Golomb, the Legion of Blue treasurer, was fired up by the festivities and summed up the night.

“I think it’s fantastic; it’s a great way for freshmen or anyone to get familiar with basketball,” the third-year Lancaster, Pennsylvania, native said. “It’s a good first step, especially for people who may be shy or afraid of going to big sporting events. It’s a good way to meet the team and feel involved.

title: ‘Endtroducing…’ new tunes to get through the midsemester grind
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
With the middle of the semester now behind us, looking at the next few weeks before Thanksgiving break means the days can start to feel blended. Our schedules are now checklists, layered with assignments and blacked-out sections designated for class and work. Free time, it seems, only exists in the passing 15 minutes between classes.

What better way to fill those gaps than with some new music? Music that will keep your mind engaged and operating on a different level. These five albums are some of the most creative and intellectual, and they’re sure to keep the gears moving smoothly in the ol’ noggin.

“Discovery” - Daft Punk

The French duo’s album, “Discovery,” is their most successful and cerebral project in their catalog. While Daft Punk completely revolutionized the EDM and house music genre with their debut album, “Homework,” “Discovery” showcased their true prowess in the field.

There's not a second on this album where you aren’t totally engaged with the synchronized beats and enchanting synths. From the classic tracks like, “One More Time,” “Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger,” and “Superheroes,” that send shockwaves through your nerves, to some of the softer tracks like “Something About Us,” “Veridis Quo,” and “Nightvision,” this album has such a stimulating effect.

Perfect for study sessions or a brisk walk back to your dorm after crushing an exam, “Discovery” will keep your mind honed in on the task at hand while keeping the vibes up — it’s brain food.

“Endtroducing…” - DJ Shadow

Following the techno route one more time is DJ Shadow’s “Endtroducing…” Released in 1996, this brain-bender is a masterclass in mixing and sampling. The album contains so much technique and specificity that you can’t help but listen in awe of the art being pumped through your headphones.

Its standout tracks, “Building Steam With a Grain of Salt,” “What Does Your Soul Look Like, Pt. 4” and “Midnight In a Perfect World,” bloom with a universe of sound and let your mind escape into a dark yet comforting world, far away from your Canvas homepage. You feel like you're floating through space, looking down on Earth and realizing how small your problems and stress really are.

Best played at the end of a long day, riding home in the back seat of a CATA bus, this album will wrap you up in a blanket of musical ambiguity to calm the hysteria of the midsemester grind.

“The Three E.P.’s” - The Beta Band

There is something about The Beta Band’s debut album that just makes sense. You can’t quite place your finger on it, you can’t quite understand why it sounds so polished, but it does. Each song sounds oddly mundane and minimal, but it’s within that simplistic style that gives it charm.

Tracks like “I Know,” “B + A” and “Push It Out,” can best be described as “alternative ambiance.” These are tracks that aren’t really songs, but rather sensible noise, like perfectly placed pieces in a mosaic puzzle.

Other tracks like “Dry the Rain,” “Dog’s Got a Bone” and “She’s the One,” have a much more traditional, lo-fi-ish sound that rocks you back with amplified lullabies. The interweaving of these two creative styles is what gives it that feeling that it just makes sense as an album.

Reserve this pick for a sunny day before the winter hits and the snow falls. You can play it in the background while working on exam guides or while looking for the next book you want to read. Either way, this album will keep your head on its toes without a second of boredom.

“Kick Out The Jams” - MC5

The Motor City Five — Talk about a band with something to say and saying it really loudly. Being one of the pioneers of the 60s Detroit protest proto-punk scene, there’s something a lot more profound about their message as a band. They represented a social movement, but a personal one as well.

In the opening track, “Ramblin’ Rose,” the band lets their “spiritual advisor,” Jesse Crawford, give a speech on behalf of the band. One of the lines in Crawford's speech is “It takes five seconds of decision, five seconds to realize your purpose on this planet.” That’s an idea to embrace and emulate both internally and externally.

Of course, the band, and this album, represent a lot within the history of the Civil Rights Movement and anti-racist protests. It's one of music’s most significant albums in terms of the nation's history at that point, while still being an incredibly intellectual and spiritually driven piece of music.

To go along with this is an unapologetic, deafening and hardcore sound that doesn’t let up throughout the 40-minute album. You feel the anger they are trying to send, like they’re using their last breaths in the heart of battle.

Save this one for when the day’s really got you down. Save it for when you forgot to hand in that assignment, for when you watch your bus leave because your professor wanted to yap about the class average of your midterm or even if you’re just annoyed that you had to get out of bed for your 9 a.m. It’ll get you through anything, really.

title: The Penn State Thespian Society 'spread a little sunshine' with 'Pippin'
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
A historically inspired story of self-discovery came to Penn State this week — the Penn State Thespian Society gave a “finale you will remember for the rest of your lives” with its performance of “Pippin” from Oct. 22-24 in Schwab Auditorium.

In the playbook, “Pippin: The Musical” is described as a very loose interpretation of the historical story of Pepin (or Pippin), the Hunchback, who was a Frankish prince and son of Charlemagne. Throughout the play, Pippin goes on a journey, searching for fulfillment and the meaning of life.

“Pippin,” has been described as a “play within a play,” as the Leading Player, played by Kaitlin McLoud, 21, of Allentown, Pennsylvania, gathers a group of players to put on the show. McLoud said her character is, at its core, a performer and wants the best for the audience.

“It was very easy to relate to her in that way and wanting people to be entertained, awestruck, to do these big things and to keep the audience engaged,” McLoud, a fourth-year studying marketing, said.

The coming-of-age story presented in the play made for a fun and engaging show that kept the audience on its toes. The actors would frequently call out or talk to the audience directly, which created a lighthearted environment that made audience members feel as though they were a part of the show.

“I actually watched the production on YouTube, and was like, ‘Wow, this show is just incredible,'” McLoud said.

Her favorite musical number to listen to from the show is “On the Right Track,” which McLoud's character performs alongside Pippin, played by Conor Barcaskey, 19, of Pittsburgh. Barcaskey, a first-year studying journalism, said the number was his favorite to sing with the Leading Player.

Barcaskey’s parents started him in the community theatre when he was 10 years old, all the way up to middle and high school, before he landed at Penn State and ultimately joined the Thespians.

“I joined because I really wanted to stay booked and busy with performing,” Barcaskey said. “ I really love it so much, and I’d love to do it in the future as a career.”

Given the fact that Barcaskey is a first-year student, he was completely shocked when he found out he was cast as Pippin, the lead role in the show. However, Barcaskey used his own experience of uncertainty as he adapts to college within his character, as Pippin is searching for his own purpose in life.

“I really use that truth in the imaginary setting of the show because I’m still trying to figure it out for myself,” Barcaskey said.

In Act II, the audience is introduced to Catherine, played by Liv Smith, 21, of State College, Pennsylvania. Smith said she relates to her character, as Catherine is just an average girl who loves deeply.

“I think the beauty of this show is finding the difference between the actor who’s playing Catherine and Catherine herself,” Smith, a second-year studying elementary and early childhood education, said. “I think I’ve been able to bring myself to both of those.”

Similarly to Barcaskey, it’s also Smith’s first year with the Thespians, but she said everyone has been nothing but supportive and welcoming. The cast members spoke highly of one another, as McLoud said her favorite thing about working with the cast is being surrounded by talented people who push her to perform her best.

“Everyone’s a family," Barcaskey said. "It’s cliché to say, … but, truly, everyone just uplifts each other. Everyone is so supportive after I exit after a number, and everybody just cheers me on. It’s such a confidence boost. It’s really awesome.”

The director of the Thespians' production of “Pippin,” Jackson Malenke, 21, of Richmond, Virginia, has been in the Thespians since his first year of college and has been working his way up from the box office ever since. Malenke, a fourth-year studying journalism, was the assistant director for the Thespians production of “Legally Blonde” in spring of 2025 and was then chosen to direct “Pippin.”

“Everyone is just great," Malenke said. "They’re my people, and even when we’re all working on a show, it just feels like we’re all hanging out, and that’s my favorite part."

title: Penn State baseball pitcher Genei Sato named Top 50 MLB Draft prospect by Baseball America
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
The hype has already started for the biggest offseason addition on the diamond.

New Penn State pitcher Genei Sato has been ranked in the Top 50 prospects for the 2027 MLB Draft. The right-handed pitcher from Kuroishi City, Japan, was ranked No. 47 overall and No.21 among right-handed pitchers.

title: What’s the national media saying about Penn State? Missing bowl game, Rocco Becht and more
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has struggled through the start of Matt Campbell’s first season in the Big Ten, and everyone is taking notice.

The Nittany Lions have lost their last four matchups, being outscored 110-74. They don’t face Ohio State or Indiana this year, resulting in an easier schedule that some predicted would finish with a College Football Playoff berth.

That possibility is now nonexistent.

Here’s a look at what national analysts are saying about Penn State and Year 1 under Campbell amidst less-than-ideal results.

Rocco Becht’s struggles

Campbell brought Rocco Becht with him to Happy Valley after starting three seasons at Iowa State. He entered the 2026 season as the winningest returning quarterback in college football and expectations were high in his final year.

But Becht has underperformed and been far from what many were hoping he’d be, leading some to wonder if he’s the right option at quarterback.

“To make matters worse, Campbell may have to consider benching fifth-year quarterback Rocco Becht, who followed him from Iowa State,” CBS’ Austin Nivison said.

Becht looked like he could be the leader Penn State needed through the three nonconference games. He had nine touchdowns and 751 yards, throwing with over 70% accuracy in the first two contests this year.

Things quickly went downhill, as he’s recorded more interceptions than touchdowns in conference play (five interceptions, three touchdowns).

“Iowa State transfer quarterback Rocco Becht was expected to be one of the reliable players on Penn State's roster this season,” Jordan Sigler of YahooSports said. “But Campbell is having to find ways to defend him in a season where he's thrown for 1,664 yards, 12 touchdowns, and five interceptions.”

Evaluating the Nittany Lions

Aside from the three nonconference wins, not much else has gone well for Campbell in his first year. And the national media has taken notice, writing in unison about the status of Penn State.

“What's not working yet: Where do we start?” ESPN’s Adam Rittenberg said. “Penn State hasn't won a Big Ten game or established a true identity on either side of the ball.”

Chris Vannini of The Athletic reranked all 138 FBS teams on Monday, with the Nittany Lions slating in at No. 62 — three places down from the week before. Penn State is below several Group of Six teams, including New Mexico (No. 40), UTSA (No. 50), North Texas (No. 55) and Memphis (No. 56).

“The Nittany Lions are still working through the year 1 struggles with Matt Campbell, but they were supposed to have an easy Big Ten schedule and be dark-horse Big Ten contenders,” Cameron Teague Robinson of The Athletic said.

Nivison graded all 18 Big Ten teams on their performance so far this season and gave the Nittany Lions the lowest grade possible — an “F.” Maryland, who fired head coach Mike Locksley on Wednesday, was the only other school to receive an F.

“The only way it could be worse was if the Nittany Lions lost one of their first three games against non-Power 4 teams,” Nivison wrote.

Remainder of the season

Penn State has five games left in its 2026 season, and it needs at least three more wins to reach the six-win bowl-eligible threshold, but even that seems difficult and far-off at the moment.

“At this rate, Penn State might be facing an uphill battle to even become bowl eligible,” Teague Robinson said.

Penn State will play Purdue, Washington, Minnesota, Rutgers and Maryland in its three-win hunt. The Scarlet Knights have just two wins this year while the Terrapins are without a permanent head coach.

But Purdue and Minnesota each have two conference victories, and Washington is 4-3 on the year. Two wins are possible for the Nittany Lions, but the third will be difficult.

“Penn State's four losses to this point include a home defeat at the hands of a middling Wisconsin team, a humiliation against Northwestern and a loss to a Michigan team that used a freshman quarterback,” Nivison said. “The Nittany Lions' manageable schedule was a reason to buy into this squad in the preseason, but now I'm wondering whether they'll even reach a bowl.

title: No. 6 Penn State women’s hockey  travels to St. Lawrence in hopes of holding win streak
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions head down to Canton, New York, to begin a six-game road trip against St. Lawrence after sweeping the Lindenwood Lions during parents' weekend.

The blue and white enter the series with plenty of momentum, having won three straight games for the first time this season. During those matches, Penn State has outscored their opponents 12-4.

Offensive depth fuels scoring surge

One of the reasons for their recent success has been the offense's ability to generate goals consistently. Since their season-opening duals against then-No. 2 Ohio State, the Nittany Lions have scored at least four goals in five of their last six games.

A great way to score goals at a high rate is to send shots to the net as often as possible, and that’s exactly what the Nittany Lions have done. Coach Jeff Kampersal has emphasized the importance of taking quality looks and converting them to goals.

“We throw it in the goalie’s stomach, and there’s no traffic around; that's kind of like a wasted shot,” Kampersal said following their second win against Lindenwood. “We could go to St. Lawrence and score eight goals because everything’s clicking.”

Things are certainly clicking for the Nittany Lion attackers, as multiple players have stepped up offensively and carved out a role for themselves. Grace Outwater was the only goal scorer through Penn State’s first two games, which raised early concern. Since then, nine players have scored. Among them are Sofia Ismael, Kylie Amelkovich and Nicole Hall, who have emerged as offensive engines.

Defensive adjustments drive second-game success

While the offense has been reliable, the Penn State defense has been quite the opposite.

The defense’s performance trend has been interesting: They struggle in the opening game of the series and succeed in the second. In their last three series, they’ve allowed a combined 11 goals in the first game compared to one goal in the second.

It’s certainly a sign that the blue and white are able to adjust well, a skill that can be attributed to both the players and the coaching staff. They showed that in their second win against Lindenwood, forcing a shutout after allowing four goals in the first match.

“We’re a really hard-working team, we just realized we need to be a little bit smarter,” Grace Outwater said. “It was just, ‘Let’s keep our heads up and make the right decision.’”

Saints' struggles hold them at a disadvantage

The blue and white hope to sustain a good enough defensive performance against a struggling St. Lawrence team that’s lost all three of its home games this season.

The Saints have faced two ranked opponents in then-No. 1 Wisconsin and then-No. 13 Clarkson University, where they’ve lost all four contests while being outscored 19-3. A clear signal that St. Lawrence struggles to compete with elite competition.

If Penn State continues to send shots to the net at a high rate, then the offense should expect goals to come in an influx.

The Saints have allowed 30.9 shots a game, which is a mark that the Nittany Lions have consistently reached. Of those shots, St. Lawrence has allowed 3.5 goals per game, showing the defense’s vulnerability throughout the season.

Penn State’s defense has a chance to gain some momentum against the Saints, who have had various mediocre offensive performances this season. The Saints have scored fewer than two goals in five of their eight matches.

Overall, a clear talent gap separates these two squads. No player on St. Lawrence’s roster stands out. Freshman forward Kendall Doiron leads the team in goals with three, while sophomore forward Cheyenne Degeer leads the team in points with six.

The Nittany Lions will look to keep the Saints in check as they search for their fourth and fifth straight win.

title: A look at the new Lady Lions coaching staff
author: Gianna Dowling | Sports Editor
description:
Only 10 days remain until the tip-off of a new era of Lady Lions basketball.

With a season ahead that brings a new-look roster and an overhauled coaching staff, the Lady Lions have plenty of chances to set the tone in this new era.

First-year head coach Tanisha Wright isn’t the only fresh face on the leadership staff, so here’s a look at the new authority group joining her on the sidelines.

Tanisha Wright

Wright returns to her alma mater for the first head collegiate coaching job of her career. The highlight of Wright’s coaching career was her stint at the helm of the Atlanta Dream from 2021-2024. During this time, she led the Dream to back-to-back playoff appearances, was named AP Coach of the Year in 2022 and coached Rhyne Howard to the second WNBA Rookie of the Year in program history.

During her time as a Lady Lion, Wright made four NCAA Tournament appearances, highlighted by a trip to the Elite Eight in 2004. She was a three-time Big Ten Defensive Player of the Year and All-Big Ten First Team selection. Wright’s 134 games played are the second-most in program history and her established collegiate career led to her being drafted No. 12 overall by the Seattle Storm in 2005.

Following her WNBA career, Wright began her coaching stint as an assistant coach at UNC Charlotte from 2017 to 2021 and also made professional stops as an assistant with the Las Vegas Aces and the Chicago Sky.

Octavia Blue

Blue comes to Happy Valley after spending the last five seasons as the head coach at Kennesaw State. She finished her stint with the Owls with a 61-89 record and coached four all-conference selections in her tenure. Blue was the fastest Kennesaw State head coach to reach 30 wins, doing so in the 2024-25 season.

Before her time with the Owls, Blue spent nine seasons at Miami, one of which was as an associate head coach. With the Hurricanes, she worked with post players and helped develop five All-ACC selections and three WNBA Draft picks.

Before Miami, Blue made stops as an assistant coach at Georgia Tech, St. John’s and St. Thomas. In her 20 years of collegiate coaching experience, Blue guided 17 all-conference selections and 25 WNBA players.

Kelly Mazzante

Joining Wright’s staff is another familiar face for Lady Lions fans. Mazzante played with Wright for three seasons and is the program's all-time leading scorer.

Mazzante returns to Happy Valley after spending the last three seasons at Georgetown, most recently as the team's associate head coach. She helped the Hoyas reach the Big East Tournament for the first time in program history, and the team appeared in the inaugural WBIT in 2024.

Before Georgetown, Mazzante was an associate head coach at Bucknell in the 2022-23 season, following three years on the Bison staff as an assistant. During this time, Bucknell made a WNIT appearance and Mazzante coached three first-team All-Patriot League selections.

Prior to Bucknell, Mazzante’s first coaching stint was as an assistant at IUP for five seasons.

Mazzante knows her way around Big Ten basketball, as a two-time conference Player of the Year and the Big Ten’s fourth all-time leading scorer for both men’s and women’s basketball.

Oliver Cadet

Cadet comes to Penn State after spending four years as the Director of Skill Development at Georgia. During his time with the Bulldogs, Cadet coached three All-SEC selections and most recently helped lead a squad to the NCAA Tournament.

Cadet also has professional experience after spending two seasons with the Atlanta Dream, in which he worked with Wright.

Susan Robinson Fruchtl

Lady Lions legend Robinson Fruchtl returns to Happy Valley as the team's Senior Director of Advancement and Strategic Relations. At Penn State, she was an All-American in 1992, Atlantic 10 Rookie of the Year in 1989, and conference Player of the Year in 1991.

Robinson Fruchtl was the captain of the 1990-91 Lady Lions squad that went 29-2 and earned the first No. 1 ranking in program history. She started her coaching career at Penn State as an assistant in 1993.

Following stints as a high school coach, Robinson Fruchtl returned to Happy Valley in 2004 under Renee Portland, where she coached Wright and Mazzante.

After Penn State, Robinson earned head coaching gigs at Saint Francis and Providence College.

title: The most accomplished Penn State athletes, and what they did after Happy Valley
author: Jimmy Blair | The Daily Collegian
description:
Many Penn State athletes across various sports have gone professional. Penn State has seen an impressive output of NFL talent in recent years and throughout its history.

However, athletes have also gone pro in other sports throughout its history. Some have forged incredible legacies that began in Happy Valley, and others are still building theirs.

Here’s a look at a few standouts.

Jesse Arnelle

Born in New Rochelle, New York, Jesse Arnelle played football and basketball for the Nittany Lions. His achievements in basketball for the school will always be legendary in Happy Valley history. He and the 1954 squad went to the NCAA Final Four that year, where he was also named an All-American. He set program records in career points and rebounds with 2,183 points and 1,238 rebounds.

“I had the most enjoyable time a student-athlete could have had,” Arnelle said to the Big Ten Conference on Feb. 15, 2008. “I love Penn State and could never do enough to repay back what it gave me. They provided me with an opportunity to find the courage and intellect within myself and start the maturing process”

After his college career, Arnelle was drafted by the Los Angeles Rams in the 1955 NFL Draft. Despite this, he chose to stick to basketball and went to the NBA. The Fort Wayne Pistons in the 1955 NBA Draft and played one season with the Pistons before retiring.

After retiring, he joined the United States Air Force and the Peace Corps. Arvelle then spent the following years of his life pursuing a career in law, in which he became a trial lawyer in the public defender's office.

Tessa Janecke

Before hitting the rink for the Nittany Lions, Tessa Janecke was preparing for a professional hockey career at the North American Hockey Academy. In her senior season, she captained her side to the tune of 46 goals and 76 assists in 78 games. In December 2018, Janecke committed to play ice hockey for Penn State.

Janecke began her career with the blue and white in 2022, and scored two goals and an assist in her debut against Wisconsin. Later on in her freshman year, she assisted on the game-winning overtime goal in the CHA championship vs. Mercyhurst. In her sophomore campaign, she scored 17 goals and 36 assists in 37 games, and led the nation in faceoff wins 607. In her senior season, she broke the program record for most points in a career by a man or women, with 141 points.

On June 17, 2026, Janecke was selected third overall by PWHL Las Vegas, which made her the first selection in franchise history. In 2025, she was selected to play for team USA in the IIHF Women’s World Championship, where she scored the game-winning goal in overtime in the gold medal game vs. Canada.

Aiden Fink

Aiden Fink, born in Calgary, began his junior career when he signed with the Brooks Bandits of the Alberta Junior Hockey League at 16.

In his two seasons with the Bandits, Fink led the team to back-to-back Centennial Cup victories, leading to the Nashville Predators drafting him 218th overall in the 2023 NHL Entry Draft.

On April 16, 2023, Aiden Fink committed to play for Penn State. He was a huge addition for the squad right away. In his freshman season for the blue and white, Fink led the team in scoring with 15 goals and 19 assists in 34 games, and he also set a single-season program record with eight power-play goals. He was named Big Ten Freshman of the Year and made the All-Conference Freshman Team.

Over his next two campaigns with the blue and white, Fink totaled 91 points in 70 games, tying for third in program history in career points and assists and sixth in goals scored.

Following the 2025-26 season, Fink signed an amateur tryout agreement with the Milwaukee Admirals, the AHL affiliate of the Predators.

Suzie McConnell-Serio

Suzie McConnell-Serio, a Pittsburgh native, played for the Penn State women’s basketball team from 1984 to 1988. In all four years, she led the conference in assists, where she would average 10.2 assists per game in her career. She also led the country in assists in her sophomore and junior seasons. In her senior year, she averaged 20.7 points per game while shooting 50% from the field. She also averaged four steals a game over her college career. By the end of her career with Penn State, she set an NCAA record for career assists with 1,307.

Following her career in Happy Valley, McConnell-Serio was selected by the Cleveland Rockers 16th overall in the 1998 WNBA draft. After her professional career, she became coach of the Minnesota Lynx in the WNBA, where she won WNBA Coach of the Year in 2004. After that stint, McConnell-Serio held various collegiate coaching roles.

Barney Ewell

In the 1940s, Barney Ewell was one of the world’s premier sprinters. By the mid-30s, he was the best sprinter-jumper in the state of Pennsylvania. After choosing to enroll at Penn State, he won 12 gold medals and championships in collegiate meets from 1940 to 1942.

He served his country from 1941 to 1945, and received his degree from the university in 1947. He was then selected for the Olympic team in 1948 after the previous two games were canceled during Ewell’s prime years. He finished second place in the 100m and 200m events, but helped the USA win gold in the 4 x 100 m relay.

He continued his athletic career in Australia after the AAU stripped him of his amateur status for accepting a furnished house in Lancaster from his fans. In 1950, he ran 100 yards in 9.5 seconds, which is the fastest pace for 100 yards in the history of Australia. Weeks later, he won the World Professional Sprint Championships in Wangaratta.

Phia Gladieux

Phia Gladieux was a monster for the Penn State field hockey team. She was a two-time conference offensive player of the year in 2022 and 2023. She led the team in points all five years she played and finished her career as Penn State’s all-time leading scorer with 94 career goals and another school record in career points with 202 points.

Gladieux was called up to the USA national team for the 2024 Paris Olympics. She scored her first Olympic goal in a 1-1 draw against Spain.

Bo Nickal

Nickal was born in Rifle, Colorado, but he grew up in Wyoming after moving with his family at a young age. He started wrestling at five years old and continued throughout high school, where he earned three Texas State Championships and committed to join Penn State during his junior.

Following his redshirt season in Happy Valley, Nickal put together one of the greatest collegiate careers in Penn State history. By the time he graduated in 2019, Nickal had an all-time record of 120-3 for the Nittany Lions, three individual national championships in 2017, 2018 and 2019, 59 career pins, and helped Penn State claim four team national championships.

Following his Penn State career, Nickal now sees himself as a middleweight mixed martial artist in the UFC. He earned his spot in the UFC through Dana White’s Contender Series in 2022. He currently has a 9-1 record and is still building his career.

title: Big Ten Tournament outlook for No. 16 Penn State women’s volleyball
author: Madelyn Lawlor | For The Collegian
description:
Two seasons on from winning a national title, it’s fair to say Penn State has fallen off the pedestal. It’s not at the echelon of the sport anymore.

After losing to Texas in the second round of the NCAA Tournament during the 2025 season, the Nittany Lions came into this season with high expectations of regaining their status at the top. Thus far, they have underperformed. But despite the challenges it has faced, Penn State still has opportunities to bounce back and have a strong postseason.

Penn State should want to avoid what happened last season, when losses in Big Ten play late in the season caused it to slide in the national rankings. The blue and white finished No. 24 in the final regular-season poll and earned an 8-seed in the NCAA Tournament, ending the season with that loss to the Longhorns.

In less than a month, the Nittany Lions will take the court for the inaugural Big Ten Tournament. The tournament presents a chance for Penn State to gain momentum and solidify its spot in the NCAA Tournament. But to seize the opportunity, it must finish strong in conference play.

Given the ups and downs of the season so far, how the Big Ten Tournament will go is up in the air. The rest of the regular season will shape that outcome. After experiencing some tough losses in conference play, the Nittany Lions have to fight through a challenging final stretch if they have any aim of doing damage in the postseason.

This year marks the first-ever Big Ten Tournament, which takes place from Nov. 20-25 in Fishers, Indiana. The top 15 of the 18 total teams in the conference make the tournament. The top four finishers in the conference earn double byes to the quarterfinals. Teams finishing fifth through ninth get a single bye. Penn State is currently 5-3 in the Big Ten, which puts it tied for fifth place in the standings and on track to earn a single bye.

The Nittany Lions had higher ambitions to start the season. Performances like the sweep against then-No. 4 Stanford in the Palestra ignited hope among the fanbase. Since entering the gauntlet of Big Ten play, the optimism has declined.

The blue and white lost to unranked Michigan State before getting swept by No. 1 Nebraska. They followed last week with a collapse against UCLA after the match was there for the taking. Even the Stanford win looks less impressive now, given that Stanford is currently only No. 15 in the national rankings, one spot ahead of the Nittany Lions.

Penn State’s wins against ranked opponents consist of that Stanford win and a win over No. 21 Washington. The Nittany Lions have lost to their other ranked opponents, including No. 4 Kentucky and No. 9 Tennessee. That trend will have to change if the blue and white want to go deep in the conference tournament.

The Nittany Lions will have plenty of opportunities in the closing stages of the regular season to add to their ranked-win tally.

With matchups against No. 10 Oregon, No. 18 Indiana, No. 12 Purdue, No. 20 Minnesota and No. 6 Wisconsin to come, Penn State will have to stack up as many wins against these teams as possible. To close the gap to conference leaders Nebraska, Oregon and Wisconsin, the blue and white should realistically look to win almost all of them.

Statistically, there are reasons for concern, but also room for improvement. Penn State’s defensive metrics such as digs per set and blocks per set could both improve. The Nittany Lions also need to improve their hitting percentage to catch up to the top teams. They currently sit 46th in the country.

By contrast, top teams the blue and white lost to, including Nebraska, Kentucky and Tennessee, all rank at the top. Notably, Michigan State — which received votes in the AVCA coaches’ poll — is also highly ranked.

If the Nittany Lions put together a strong resume to close the season, beat the teams they’re expected to beat and string together a couple of challenging wins against ranked opponents, they’ll be in a good place to start the Big Ten Tournament.

Penn State can build momentum in this closing stretch of the season. If it does, it’ll have a chance of going deep into the conference tournament. This would also put the blue and white in a better place for NCAA tournament seeding.

If Penn State continues to struggle to close out matches, especially against teams lower in the conference standings, it’ll have to be perfect against the remaining Big Ten slate to maintain its position in the conference and prevent a slide out of the single-bye slots.

The Nittany Lions get their next opportunity to change the narrative Friday against Oregon. If it comes away with a win, Penn State could be dangerous in the Big Ten Tournament. A loss would mean another setback relative to the top teams in the conference.

Penn State’s current resume doesn’t inspire confidence. But it still has a chance to build momentum over the coming matches. If the Nittany Lions can do that, they can go deep in the Big Ten Tournament and even set their sights on winning it.
