title: Column | Legalized synthetic cannabinoids are at the forefront of the new Drug War
author: Quentin Jurney | The Daily Collegian
description:
Gas stations are some of the most convenient stores in America; they’re open at all hours and carry a variety of supplies to offer a quick fix to a range of issues. However, they also carry goods that are more harmful than food or gas: Tobacco products and, more recently, THC derivatives or synthetic cannabinoids.

The history of THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) derivatives is a complex, interesting story. It started in 2018, when Congress passed the Agriculture Improvement Act, legalizing hemp nationwide by removing it from the Federal Controlled Substances Act. Hemp is legally classified as Marijuana with less than 0.3% delta-9 THC, the psychoactive compound in weed.

This was seen as a step forward in marijuana legislation since it dropped hemp and hemp seeds from the Drug Enforcement Administration's (DEA) Schedule I controlled substances list. This means farmers and regular Americans have the ability to order hemp and hemp seeds for a variety of reasons, such as food, fiber for clothes, paper, rope, mulch and hempcrete, a bio-composite construction material.

The 2018 bill also allowed the legal shipment and transportation of hemp and hemp-derived products across state lines, and made licensed hemp growers eligible for federal crop insurance, disaster assistance and farm loans through the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

This bill seems full of positives, with little to no drawbacks; it helps many people and encourages the use of hemp over many less sustainable or environmentally friendly products.

However, unsavory actors and gray markets found a loophole within the 2018 Farm Bill. It specifically mentions delta-9 THC was still banned federally, but people realized there are many other psychoactive compounds in weed.

“Cannabis contains more than 100 cannabinoids, and the broader THC family includes delta-8, delta-10, THCA, THCV, THCP, and other closely related compounds,” according to Weedmaps, a tech company that connects users to local dispensaries.

These compounds have been overlooked for decades, since they were only found in minuscule amounts in the Cannabis flower and bud; there was no point in looking deeper into them, because you couldn't use them to get high. Now, with modern technology, it’s made extremely easy to extract or manufacture large amounts of these compounds through synthetic means.

Since all these compounds were found in small amounts, they were disregarded when formatting the 2018 Farm Bill. So when hemp was legalized, all these other cannabinoids, excluding the classic delta-9 THC, were legalized as well, dumping dozens of synthetic cannabinoids on the legal market.

All of these new substances were legalized with little oversight and little testing of both the product itself and the methods used to extract and manufacture these cannabinoids. Since this loophole was first exploited, these synthetic THC derivatives have exploded everywhere in the U.S., most commonly sold at gas stations and convenience stores where other gray market items are sold.

However, even dispensaries regulated by the Pennsylvania government use THC-A, a naturally occurring THC derivative. This derivative turns into THC when heated up, thus having the same effect when smoked.

There has been little research done on these new compounds, since they hit the market relatively recently, but the research conducted so far has yielded some unnerving results. Quality control is inadequate in the newly emerging THC industry. Consumers are ingesting products that are mislabeled with compounds that have never received any toxicological testing; and EVALI cases continue to be reported with a fatality rate approaching 2% in California, a study from the National Library of Medicine concluded.

EVALI, an E-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury, was first identified in 2019. It’s sometimes referred to as vaping-associated pulmonary injury or vaping-associated lung injury. EVALI is an acute or subacute respiratory illness and can be fatal, according to the American Lung Association.

Another study done by the National Library of Medicine showed that none of the synthetic THC products tested were labeled correctly and many had unlabeled additives and harmful chemicals. When looking at 27 products from 10 brands, none were found to have accurate labeling, with 11 products containing unlabeled cutting agents. These studies essentially concluded that there were so many unknown chemicals found and not labeled in THC derivatives, you have no way of knowing what’s in them when you buy them.

A lot of the people responsible for the production of synthetic cannabinoids don’t follow any safety regulations when it comes to safe extraction or chemical manufacturing of these psychotropics, letting many harmful chemicals into the final products. Yes, that's right: Many times THC derivatives aren’t extracted from hemp but rather chemically manufactured in a lab, which somehow is still allowed in this loophole. Both these methods have caused adverse health risks, and even death in some instances.

This has been found to be a problem not only in manufacturing methods, but also in the product itself. “National poison control centers received 2,362 exposure cases of delta-8 THC products between January 1, 2021, and February 28, 2022. Of the 2,362 exposure cases: 58% involved adults, 41% involved pediatric patients less than 18 years of age, and 1% did not report age. 40% involved unintentional exposure to delta-8 THC and 82% of these unintentional exposures affected pediatric patients,” according to the Federal Drug Administration.

These products are concentrated in such high doses they’ve become lethal. Because of their widespread legality and availability, children can become easily exposed, causing hospitalizations and even deaths.

The concept of someone dying from weed was thought to be almost impossible before now. No deaths from overdose of marijuana have been reported, according to the United States Drug Enforcement Administration. Synthetic cannabinoids have completely changed the landscape when it comes to marijuana, making it much more harmful.

As a student at Penn State, you have access to these THC derivatives. My advice: stay far away from them. From mislabeling, to problems in the synthesizing process to the pure potency of it, it's just such a dangerous and stupid activity.

You literally have no idea what you're putting in your body and how it will affect you. I know it’s legal, and a lot of people use that as a justification, but it’s only legal through loopholes, and many shady actors are taking advantage of that.

Gas station weed is a risky substance to put in your body. You might be fine and have a grand old time being high, but you risk death or life-altering medical conditions. Playing Russian roulette with your life doesn’t seem like a good price to pay just to get high.

MORE COLUMNS

title: Newly opened store JoLife brings Asian lifestyle items to State College
author: Colleen Cratty | The Daily Collegian
description:
Asian pop culture has been seeping into the American mainstream for years, from the popularity of KPop Demon Hunters and Squid Game to Korean skincare and Sanrio stationary and bento boxes.

Happy Valley is no stranger to the nationwide trends. Jolife, a Japanese lifestyle store, opened Oct. 3 in downtown State College. The shop sells a variety of products for any occasion, like international snacks, beauty items, popular collectables and more.

Located on South Allen Street, the store is filled with trending items from all over Asia. Most notably, it has blind boxes and mini-figures, like Sonny Angels and Smiskis, which have become popular in the last few years.

“Students are excited because products that they only sell in Japan, they can find here,” Tiffany Lu, the store’s owner, said.

Lu, 35, of China, said she decided to open a store in State College because of the value it could bring to students. She said the origin of the store’s name is to encourage customers to “enjoy life.”

“It’s a very special store in this very special place,” Lu said. “State College has a great environment.”

Lu mentioned that students have been most interested in Jolife's figurines and beauty products. She said that a lot of young people know of these items from social media, like TikTok and Instagram, so there’s been plenty of quick interest in what her shop has to offer.

At the front of the store, a display showcases the variety of collectables and blind boxes available for purchase. Customers can see all types of toys and surprises they can get in glass cases, but ultimately, they have no idea what product they will end up with.

Blind boxes have been a huge trend in Japan for years, stemming from the tradition of fukubukuro on New Year's — bags with unknown contents that, according to tradition, bring good luck for the following year.

In the 2010s, the brand Pop Mart brought blind boxes to the mainstream, and now with the help of social media, the products have taken off. Last year, Labubus exploded in popularity, becoming a staple in blind box culture and fashion.

“I prefer the blind box section because I always like to open the mystery boxes,” Sunny Li, a Jolife worker, said. “I don’t know what is in there, so I love waiting for the surprise.”

Li, a third-year studying linguistics, said the store’s snacks have been incredibly popular, too, specifically its variety of ice cream — mango, strawberry and other fruit-shaped ones can be found in coolers at the back of the store, along with aisles of international candies, ramen and chips.

Beyond the rows and rows of snacks, customers can find stationary, beauty products and other knick-knacks to browse and buy.

Chahak Goswami, a customer at the store, said she was excited about the ice cream, as she had previously tried them at home.

“There’s a huge variety of products, but it still doesn’t overstimulate me,” Chahak Goswami, a second-year student studying artificial intelligence methods and applications, said. “The store calms me down and relaxes me.”

A lot of women come to the store specifically looking for Japanese and Korean beauty products, Lu said, as they’ve been trending online. The foundation products are particularly beloved by students, she added.

Korean skincare and beauty products can be traced back to the Three Kingdoms period of Korea. Modern Korean beauty products began to emerge at the end of the 19th century, and after a ban on imported products in 1961, the Korea’s beauty market began to grow exponentially.

It spread to the United States in the 2000s with the popularity of K-pop and K-drama. Among American audiences, Korean beauty suddenly became a staple in cosmetic stores in the states.

K-beauty staples like BB creams can be found at Jolife, as well as a variety of cosmetics from other Asian countries.

Li, 20, of China, said having a huge range of products was a priority for Jolife. She added that they hope to have new products come in every month.

“I want to give them new, fresh memories about our store,” Li said. “I don’t want the store to stay always the same items. Then, people will come again and again.”

Li mentioned that the store has just started planning for the upcoming holiday season, and will hopefully host special events around Thanksgiving and Christmas. She said that these events will include games for customers to enjoy together.

Lu said the purpose of the store is to share Asian culture with the people of State College, as well as make Asian students feel more at home. Similarly, Li said it was exciting to have a store like Jolife open locally.

“This kind of store is very popular in New York and Los Angeles,” Li said. “But I think in State College, they need this store for the young people and students.”

title: Penn State women’s soccer tops No. 5 Michigan State in nail-biting finish
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Battling in East Lansing, Michigan, at the DeMartin Soccer Complex, Penn State and No. 5 Michigan State faced off in a tough conference matchup.

Coming into the game, the Nittany Lions won seven of the last eight meetings with the Spartans, leading the series at 26-7-0.

Penn State took a 2-1 lead over Michigan State, continuing their all-time series dominance over the Spartans.

The green and white started fast, quickly moving to the blue and white’s final third after the opening whistle.

Kayla Briggs drew a foul on Molly Martin just outside Penn State’s 18-yard box in the third minute. Renee Watson took the free kick for Michigan State but skied it way over the top left side of the net.

Emma Johnson created the first Nittany Lion shot of the match in the 11th minute. The freshman from Greenfield, Indiana, blew past Bella Najera with explosive footwork and placed a shot in the bottom center of the net that Noelle Henning ultimately saved.

In the 19th minute, Aubrey Kulpa created a goal-scoring opportunity off a long ball from Penn State’s defensive end but could not place it past the Spartans’ back line. The blue and white continued their offensive pressure, totaling four shots on goal at the midway point of the first half.

Bella Ayscue and Briggs found themselves in a tussle in the 23rd minute after gaining possession in the midfield. Ayscue went down hard and was assessed for injuries to her right leg but was able to run off the field.

Najera had a scary opportunity just inside Penn State’s eighteen after receiving a cross from Ava Lutke on the left side. The senior midfielder took a wide-open, one-touch shot that Kayleigh Herr blocked just in time.

“When we started 1v1, they were bringing a second defender pretty quick. There's just not really much space in there to be able to find to get going forward,” Michigan State coach Jeff Hosler told The State News. “Penn State's really good at closing down spaces, blocking shots, (and) did a great job of that in the first half especially.”

After the dangerous Michigan State attack, Ayscue found herself on the ground again, irritated in the same right leg. The junior defender had to limp off the pitch this time around.

Despite Ayscue's loss, the Nittany Lions kept up the offensive pressure.

Kulpa gained possession at the top of the Spartan’s eighteen and connected with Paige Kalal on the right flank. Kalal fired a shot to the far left corner of the net, placing it past Henning, putting the blue and white up 1-0 in the 35th minute.

The Penn State goal lit a fire under the green and white for the final 10 minutes of the first 45. Michigan State found themselves consistently pressuring the Nittany Lions just outside their six-yard box but could not capitalize, keeping the blue in white in the lead 1-0 heading into the second half.

Penn State opened up the second half fast with a quick goal in the 46th minute. Back in the game with a knee brace, Bella Ayscue cleared the ball from the Nittany Lion defensive end and found Kulpa’s feet at midfield. Kulpa broke away from Spartan defender Samantha Maroni on a long breakaway and sniped the bottom left corner with a powerful shot, putting the blue and white up 2-0.

After the Penn State goal, the green and white found extra energy once again on the offensive end. Watson gained possession at the half and bulldogged her way down to just before the Nittany Lion’s eighteen.

The senior defender found Briggs on the right wing, who was able to get past both Herr and Gress to shrink the deficit to 2-1 in the 54th minute.

Briggs almost found the back of the net again in the 61st minute but misplaced it just over the crossbar.

Michigan State continued its offensive dominance, creating its 6th corner kick opportunity in the 74th minute. The Spartans proved time and time again why they average 8.53 corner kicks per match this season.

The green and white almost had a game-changing opportunity when challenging a potential handball on Ayscue in the blue and white’s eighteen. The challenge was ultimately dismissed in the 78th minute. With the Spartans looking to draw even, Penn State continued to put players behind the ball and set up a low block to prevent scoring chances.

“It's been a familiar tactic; everybody we've played for three weeks, maybe going on four, has been set up in a low block for most of the game against us, putting numbers in behind it,” Hosler told The State News. “Obviously the difficult part is when you go down like now, they're just going to be even more compact and tougher to break down.”

Coach Hosler challenged yet another play in Penn State’s eighteen, looking to be awarded a penalty kick from a potential foul on Emma Johnson. Their second and final challenge was denied again.

Despite Michigan State’s repeated pressure, the Spartans couldn’t find the equalizer. Penn State took the game at 2-1.

Up next

Penn State stays on the road but doesn’t go far, facing No. 24 Michigan Sunday at 1 p.m.

title: State College borough holds open house to inspire more public input on roadway safety initiative
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Several State College residents came to the community room of the borough’s municipal building on Wednesday for an open house to learn more about an ongoing initiative that seeks to make State College’s roads safer.

Having started in June, the initiative, titled Vision Zero, aims to eliminate traffic deaths and injuries in State College. It expands on the work done as part of the Next Generation Safety and Mobility Plan, which the borough adopted in March 2024, with support from funds from a Safe Streets and Roads for All grant from the Department of Transportation.

Currently in its second phase, the plan for Vision Zero is expected to be completed in April 2027. A draft of the plan, which will use data from recorded crashes within the borough and road safety concerns gathered from public comments, is also expected to be presented to the State College Borough Council for review.

State College transportation engineer and Vision Zero project manager Ron Seybert said the data being collected will also be used to refine a map of where traffic deaths and injuries are most likely to occur in State College. The map will then be used along with the rest of Vision Zero’s findings to inform considerations on where the borough should construct road safety measures such speed bumps, raised medians and speed feedback signs to lower crash and injury rates on State College’s roadways.

He said public comment is pivotal to this effort by ensuring that these safety measures are put in places where residents, and not just data, say they need to go.

“If we're doing projects that are publicly funded, people should have an opportunity to review and comment on them,” Seybert said. “I think we're gonna find that this information is going to align with what we're seeing here to validate it — I'll be surprised if we see much here that's different from that.”

Kevin Kassab, a member of the State College Borough Council, said he often feels more lighting is required at busy intersections in State College so pedestrians are able to better be seen by passing vehicles.

He said this and other traffic concerns were expressed by attendees of the open house and felt holding more of them would allow for more exposure and understanding of how Vision Zero plans to address them.

“It's critical that we bring people in and I think it's critical that they feel that they're part of the decision making of what we do to ensure the safety of our visitors and our residents within State College. When I talk to people, they appreciate those open houses; it gives them that opportunity,” Kassab, 68, of State College, Pennsylvania, said. “You can sit and write, make a list of things, but sometimes it's better just to meet the people that are working on the program so that you can get your questions answered pretty quickly.”

Cynthia Carpenter, who lives in College Heights, said she heard about the open house from an email notification announcing it. She said she has heard of several crashes occurring on North Atherton Street, especially along its intersection with Park Avenue, and feels that more needs to be done to reduce traffic in the area.

She said while she didn’t hear much about how Vision Zero would make this intersection safer, the initiative's discussion on how to improve safety for pedestrians and cyclists was something Carpenter could get behind.

However, she pointed out the need for Vision Zero to also take into account the proliferation of electric bikes and scooters throughout Pennsylvania, which she said she thought would require some “creative thought” when considering solutions for making these modes of transportation safer to use in the borough.

“People are still gonna use cars, but others are using other modes and they need to be safe,” Carpenter, 60, of State College, Pennsylvania, said.

Laurie Mulvey, 62, of State College, Pennsylvania, also learned about the open house via email and found it "unusual" for a local government to handle so proactively when there are other issues that take priority and attributed this level of attention to the resources currently at the borough’s disposal to fund the project.

Having expressed a desire to see areas in State College with many cross streets and residential areas, such as Pugh Street, be made safer to travel, as well as an end to a “pattern” of accidents occurring along the intersection of South Pugh Street and Easterly Parkway, Mulvey said the only way for Vision Zero to truly address these issues was through the public spreading the word about them.

“Maybe I'm the only person who thinks that there's a problem at that intersection, but if there's 25 people or 100, then you're gonna say, ‘oh, that's notable,’ but if nobody comes, you'll never know,” Mulvey said. ”You could be the best expert, but you can't see everything, no matter what, and so you just need people.”

title: Penn State hosts Canisius in final nonconference series before Big Ten play
author: Dominic Megats I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is still looking to add to the win column after starting its season 0-4 for only the second time in program history.

The Nittany Lions fell to Robert Morris 5-2 on Tuesday to start a three-game homestand.

After dropping its second-straight home game, the blue and white must turn their attention to Canisius. The Golden Griffins enter Pegula Ice Arena for Game 1 at 7 p.m. Friday.

Disciplinary problems

Penn State had no problem coming out of the gates hot against then-No. 8 Quinnipiac in its lone game against them. It was quite the opposite against the Colonials on Tuesday. The main reason behind the disparity: penalties.

The Nittany Lions gave up four penalties in the first period against Robert Morris, including one that led to a power-play goal. They quickly fell behind 3-0 to open the contest after spending most of the period against a man advantage.

Discipline problems weren’t only noticeable in their previous game. The Bobcats were on the power-play seven times and found the back of the net four times.

“I feel it’s arrogance. I feel that we feel we’re above what we had to do in the past to get where we got,” Guy Gadowsky said following the 5-2 loss to Robert Morris. “That’s how I feel, and obviously that’s on me because that’s a preparation issue, so that’s absolutely on me and myself and our staff.”

With all the penalties coming the Nittany Lions way, it’s been up to the penalty kill unit to seemingly decide if they can stay in games or not. Penn State killed 72% of penalties so far in the season, ranking it among the worst in the NCAA.

Beyond discipline issues, the blue and white still don’t have a clear starter in net. Both Ryder Fetterolf and Josh Fleming are off to similar starts. The two netminders have a 4.1 goals-against average through two games each.

However, one shining light in what’s been a dim start to the season has been the newcomers. Justin Poirier was the lone goal scorer against the Colonials. The Maine transfer found the back of the net twice and showed off his powerful shot in the process.

“(Poirier’s) shot is incredible; it’s fun to watch… (I) absolutely love the way he shoots the puck,” Gadowsky said. “He had surgery in the offseason; it’s been a long road back, and it’s still getting there. But you can see every week he’s getting a little more and more comfortable. When he gets open and can shoot the puck, he’s as dangerous as any player there is.”

Scouting Canisius

Coming into town is a team that's been back-and-forth to start the season. Canisius started the season 2-0-1 with a tie to Ferris State. Although starting the year undefeated, the Golden Griffins may be on cooldown at the right time for Penn State.

Rhys Chiddenton and Noah Quinn led their team with five points each. Chiddenton is one of two Canisius returners to finish in the top five in scoring. Quinn is a new addition from Bemidji State. The senior is spending his lone season as a Golden Griffin after recording 15 points in 62 games for the Beavers.

Jack Lisson seems to have earned the starting role between the pipes for Canisius. The freshman currently has a 2.05 goals-against average and a .926 save percentage. The Oakville, Ontario, native let in five goals on 29 shots in his last start.

There’s no question the Nittany Lions must use the weekend to bounce back against a struggling team after a humbling start to their season. An unforgiving conference slate is approaching, as this will be the last opportunity for Penn State to prepare for Big Ten competition.

MORE HOCKEY COVERAGE

title: From Penn State teammates to business partners, the Clifford brothers’ paths continue
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Growing up playing football, Liam Clifford never thought he’d follow his older brother, Sean, to Penn State. Sean had arrived in Happy Valley in 2017, and Liam wanted to carve out his own path in college football.

But when Clifford attended a camp at Penn State ahead of his junior year of high school and received a scholarship offer from then-coach James Franklin, his perspective changed.

“For some reason, it just felt way different after that moment,” Clifford told The Daily Collegian. “Why would you want to go anywhere else? You’ve got your brother here, you’ve got a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. It was just an opportunity I couldn’t pass up, and I’m glad I didn’t. I wouldn’t trade it for the world.”

While the two played football together growing up, they never shared the field in high school. So, their reunion at Penn State allowed them to compete with one another and hold themselves to a high standard together.

The two brothers ultimately spent two years together at Penn State from 2021-22. It was an opportunity for them to play collegiate football, but it was a way for them to grow closer on and off the field too.

“They had that relationship where if one person isn’t doing what the other person thinks is their full potential, they’re gonna get on each other,” Brandon Smith, a Penn State linebacker from 2019 to 2021, told the Collegian. “Just seeing that was very confident to know their dynamics and how much they really pushed each other and cared for success.”

Clifford redshirted his freshman year at Penn State in 2021, and Sean threw for a career-high 3,107 yards but led the Nittany Lions to just a 7-6 record.

Sean had one more year to hopefully bounce back from the lackluster season, but 2022 didn’t come without adversity, as the Nittany Lions lost to Michigan and Ohio State.

Against the Wolverines, Sean had just a 36.8% completion percentage, while he threw three interceptions in the defeat to the Buckeyes.

“Shortcomings and disappointments are one of those things that life brings,” Smith said. “If (Sean) had a bad play, he’s going to come right back at you harder than he did before because that’s just who he is.”

But Sean ended up leading Penn State to its first Rose Bowl victory since 1995 that year, defeating Utah 35-21. While he didn’t find a connection with his little brother during the game, the two linked up twice for nine yards throughout the season.

“I always just wanted to play big time college football and Penn State gave me that platform to be able to do that at the highest level possible,” Sean told The Daily Collegian. “Some of the biggest things you could ever dream of when it comes to White Out (games), the Rose Bowl and all those different things, I got a chance to play in, and I wouldn’t change it for the world.”

After six seasons in Happy Valley and two years with his brother, Sean’s time putting on the Penn State jersey was over. But it was far from the last time he and Clifford would partner together.

During Sean’s final year in college, the two co-founded Limitless NIL, the first NIL agency founded by student-athletes. At a time where NIL opportunities and collectives were becoming more prominent, Clifford said “it was just something that we were passionate about.”

“We saw an opportunity in the market, a new market really at the time in NIL, and being able to attack that while also helping student athletes, specifically starting at Penn State,” Clifford said. “Expanding beyond Penn State was just something that was a lot of fun and became a passion of ours.”

The opportunities continued to grow in the business world for the brothers. Clifford took over as CEO of Limitless NIL after Sean graduated and sold off the company after graduating.

From there, they veered into venture capital, investing in “anything that advances human health, human performance, or human potential,” Clifford said. They co-founded Clifford Capital and The New Era Fund, targeting smaller startups seeking validation from athletes and coaches that are trying to enter the sports world.

“(Limitless NIL) ignited that entrepreneurial flame,” Clifford said. “Now, being able to do that with the companies we invest in and the portfolio we're building and continuing to build, venture capital is entrepreneurship on (steroids).”

While the business opportunities gave the Cliffords an avenue outside of football, Sean compared the hustle and grind the founders have to what he experienced as an athlete. He referred to the Latin meaning of passion: to suffer.

“I’ve just always been drawn to the fact that these founders are no different than athletes, and bringing those both together has been really cool,” Sean said. “I think that’s going to be a hell of a story as we continue to write it.”

As their business ventures continued to grow, the brothers found themselves navigating a different kind of uncertainty, this time in professional football.

Sean was selected in the fifth round of the 2023 NFL Draft by the Green Bay Packers, while Clifford signed as an undrafted free agent with the Indianapolis Colts in 2026.

They faced significant adversity in the big leagues, as Sean bounced between the practice squad and active roster with the Packers before ending up with the Cincinnati Bengals, where he’s also seen up-and-down movement.

Clifford, meanwhile, worked out with the Colts for two weeks before he was cut, was signed by the Los Angeles Chargers then released again before the season began.

“You always have to reintroduce yourself each and every time and be able to show this is the new and improved me every single time,” Smith said. “That’s one of the things I’ve been able to witness seeing Sean and different opportunities he’s been granted with, and also seeing Liam and the different things he’s been able to accomplish.”

New opportunities to prove himself haven’t always been available for Clifford, but he’s embraced the experience of being in the NFL and continues to work for another chance.

“I’m staying in shape, I’m staying ready,” Clifford said. “I’m going with the flow, but in the meantime, every other waking hour I have that I’m not working out and training, I’m putting into the business. The hard work and the busy days and the busy schedules is what continues to drive me.”

Whether the brothers are playing in the NFL or meeting with investors, the processes and interactions have been the same. Sean compared detecting the right markets and perfecting ad campaigns to finding his wide receivers on the football field.

“There is a bit of luck that comes at all of us,” Sean said. “Do everything in their power to make everything work, and then it completely and utterly flops. But at the end of the day, it's getting shots on goal. It's doing what you can beforehand to prepare.”

Much of that preparation came at Penn State — the place that set them on the right path for the NFL and their business ventures.

It's been four years since Sean has suited up for the Nittany Lions and only one season since Clifford has worn the blue and white, but their love for Penn State stays strong.

“Penn State gave me everything,” Clifford said. “Coach Franklin gave me one of the coolest opportunities to play in front of 107,000 people every weekend. But beyond that, just the relationships, what the school had to offer and just being in a place like State College where the community is just so tight knit, it's the most fun place to play in the entire world.”

title: Pros, cons of the expanded 24-team College Football Playoff
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Well, it happened. The College Football Playoff will likely be expanding to 24 teams in 2027, with the organization striking a “handshake deal” with ESPN to widen the field, according to multiple reports.

ESPN will be paying $345 million each year, but they’ll be paying just $205 million in theory after getting back about $140 million annually from the cancellation of the three conference championship games the network carries.

This comes just three seasons into the 12-team CFP, which many felt was the “sweet spot” after a decade of the four-team playoff.

If the field had been 24 teams since the format began in 2014, Penn State would’ve made the playoffs seven times. It has only made the CFP once in 2024, the first year there were 12 teams.

Here are the unknowns, pros and cons of the expanded field.

Unknowns

What happens to the lower-level bowl games?

Every six-win team in college football is always eligible for a bowl game. The New Year’s Six bowls — the Rose Bowl, Peach Bowl, Sugar Bowl, Fiesta Bowl, Orange Bowl and Cotton Bowl — have been reserved for the CFP since the expansion to 12 teams, and that won’t change under the new format, either.

It’s the future of the lower-tier bowls that becomes murky with the 24-team field. They were already losing their value with a 12-team playoff (i.e. Notre Dame opted out of the Pop Tarts Bowl after missing the CFP last year), but now their value could fall even further.

Potential realignment or independents?

The Big Ten and SEC are undoubtedly going to be the beneficiaries of this expansion. They are widely regarded as the two best conferences and therefore will get more teams in the field each year compared to the Big 12 and ACC.

So what’s stopping some of the better teams in the other conferences from trying to join the already massive Big Ten and SEC?

But arguably the biggest winner of the new format is Notre Dame. The Fighting Irish are one of two independent teams in college football, which means they get to create their own schedule, giving them the opportunity to schedule easier Power Four opponents.

Some other schools could decide being independent is the best way to move forward in this new era, as those programs would get their own media rights deals and freedom to schedule whichever teams they please.

Pros

More competitive regular season games

With more wiggle room to make the playoffs could potentially mean better regular season matchups, as most of the top programs currently choose to schedule Group of Six or FCS teams for free wins at the beginning of the year.

SEC commissioner Greg Sankey initially said he would only agree to a 24-team playoff if every team had to schedule 10 Power Four games. It’s unclear whether that condition is included in this agreement.

More on-campus playoff games

The first round games in the 12-team format were held on college campuses, and to say they were electric would be an understatement.

Now, the first two rounds of the CFP will be held at the higher seed’s home stadium, giving fans more chances to have an impact on their team’s playoff journey and create some unforgettable atmospheres.

Cons

Regular season games mean less

Two losses put teams on the edge of the 12-team playoff, three basically eliminated them. Now, three defeats in the Big Ten or SEC keeps a program in the field.

Winning used to mean so much more in college football. One loss would nearly kick someone out of the four-team playoff. Fans would be on the edge of their seats for every single game.

The Kick Six? Wouldn’t have mattered in the grand scheme of national championship aspirations. Stanford’s win over USC in 2007? The Trojans are likely still making the CFP. The implications of so many of the most memorable moments in college football’s history would be reduced to nothing.

The regular season just means less with the expanded field. There’s no way around it. Well, unless you’re a team in the ACC or Big 12, as the committee always seems to judge those losses harder.

No more conference championships

The SEC championship has long been one of the greatest games of the college football season. It’s consistently one of the most watched matchups, and it was the first-ever conference championship created in football, forever changing the landscape of the sport.

With the CFP expansion, it’s gone. So are the Big Ten championship, the ACC championship and the Big 12 championship.

Conference championship weekend has produced some of the greatest moments in college football, and Penn State’s 2016 Big Ten championship win is one of the biggest accomplishments the Nittany Lions have had since the Joe Paterno era.

It’s going to be weird without them. And these games are also the reason why the CFP expansion isn’t actually producing that much extra revenue for ESPN and other stakeholders.

title: ‘Everything should be max effort’ | Andrew Destin reflects on journey to The Athletic
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
In 2018, Andrew Destin toured Penn State in the midst of a late-spring State College blizzard. A week earlier, he toured his father’s alma mater, Cal Poly, on a contrastingly gorgeous day in southern California.

Battling the elements, he tucked into The Daily Collegian’s office and, at the suggestion of his parents, chatted with some of the staffers inside.

“I remember walking outside the building, and I went back into that sh—ty weather, where it was snowy and cold and windy,” Destin said. “I turned to my parents, and I was like, ‘Damn it!’ And they're like, ‘What? What is it?’ I was like, ‘I have to go here.’”

Now a full-time reporter, Destin has worked for several highly regarded sports journalism publications since graduating from Penn State in 2022. His journey started at the college paper.

“That visit to the Collegian office, it told me that I wanted to be a sports reporter,” Destin said. “That's what I wanted to do one day, and here I am, still doing it.”

Destin grew up in Saratoga, California, a suburb of San Jose not far from Levi’s Stadium, the home of the San Francisco 49ers.

A die-hard college football fan, he’d wake up at 6 a.m. on autumn Saturdays to catch the beginning of College GameDay. And as the child of two parents who met in a Penn State MBA program, he made the five-hour drive to Pasadena for the Nittany Lions’ Rose Bowl losses to USC in 2009 and 2017.

He was never one for video games or YouTube. Instead, when a young Destin was stressed, avoiding homework or simply sitting at the dining table before school, he’d peruse a copy of the San Francisco Chronicle or San Jose Mercury News.

Thanksgiving football was a big deal for the Destin family, and after one year’s iteration, he recapped the action by writing a game story in a spiral notebook.

“That was the first inkling of like, ‘Wow, he's doing this,’” Maureen Destin, his mother, said. “Some kids don't like to write. He was doing that for fun.”

Destin initially envisioned other careers, but his focus shifted toward journalism in high school. As a varsity baseball and basketball player, it seemed like the best way to keep pursuing his passion for athletics.

“It kind of dawned on me, after I got a B in freshman biology, that being a marine biologist maybe wasn't in store,” Destin said. “I realized I am a good athlete; I am not a great athlete. If I am going to stick with sports, the best way to do it is to go to games.”

So Destin headed to Happy Valley and forfeited the Golden State’s picture-perfect sunshine for the unpredictable meteorological patterns of Centre County. At the Collegian, Destin held roles as a sports editor and men’s hockey reporter. He also served as a CommRadio sports director and play-by-play broadcaster for Big Ten Plus.

Destin interned with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette the summer before his senior year, then covered the Nittany Lions’ football team for the same outlet upon returning in the fall. Toward the end of his time in college, he earned the opportunity to cover Super Bowl LVI in Los Angeles.

“When you become a really professional journalist at a very young age, it can lose the luster of it a little bit,” Destin said. “Yes, it's good to be professional. It's good to be mature. It's also really good to still be like, ‘Hey, this is really freaking cool. I'm covering the Super Bowl.’ That's something I've had to learn as I've pursued my career.”

Noah Hiles was working for the Beaver County Times in 2022 when he heard rumors that a position on the Post-Gazette’s Penn State beat would soon be opening up. He expected to have a shot at the job, but was surprised to learn the paper already had a candidate in mind.

That candidate, of course, was Destin.

“I was kind of annoyed,” Hiles said. “I was like, ‘Who the heck is this kid? He's in college.’ And it turned out (that) he ended up being probably the best young reporter that I've ever worked with, and also one of my best friends.”

Hiles still ended up at the Post-Gazette, covering Pitt instead, and would co-host a podcast with Destin as the duo wrote about the in-state rivals.

Eventually the paper decided it was no longer interested in having a full-time Penn State reporter, and Destin shifted into a role where he’d split time on its Pirates and Penguins beats. About a year later, Hiles got a similar promotion and began partnering with Destin at PNC Park.

Together, they formed a dynamic reporting duo. In the year that Destin and Hiles shared on the Pirates beat, they combined their skill sets to break news and get scoops that other outlets weren’t able to.

“We were both young and hungry,” Hiles said. “We were so sourced, we had our fingerprints all over that organization and we could find out anything.”

In the process, the Mount Union alum also saw Destin further develop as a journalist. Ahead of writing a story on star Pirates pitcher Paul Skenes, Destin was careful to make a connection with the ace before proceeding, which Hiles pointed to as a moment that embodied his skill on the beat.

“He was just so smart,” Hiles said. “Before reaching out to the family, he had the wherewithal to ask Paul for permission, and Paul appreciated that so much. I think Andrew was the first guy's name on the beat that Paul took the time to learn.”

After spending years in Pennsylvania, Destin looked onward to opportunities back on the West Coast and broke the news to Hiles during a spring-training round of golf in Bradenton, Florida.

“He was telling me about his interviews that he had lined up,” Hiles said. “I just said, ‘This is really it, huh?’ And he was like, ‘Yeah.’”

In April 2025, Destin moved to Seattle after accepting a role at the Associated Press, a new gig where he’d cover sports throughout Washington.

In the process, though, he started to struggle. Earlier in the year, he was diagnosed with mental health conditions including anxiety, depression and insomnia.

“It was all very rapid onset,” Destin said. “I went from highly productive, highly functioning, mentally doing great and within like three, four or five months, got insanely burnt out.”

Coupled with the many responsibilities that came with the new role, it made for a tough start to his time in the Emerald City. But he persevered. From late 2025 through the summer of 2026, Destin worked at some of the world’s highest-profile sporting events.

After covering the Seattle Mariners’ ALCS appearance, he made his way to Levi’s Stadium and covered the Seahawks’ victory in Super Bowl LX, not far from his childhood home. Then, he worked the several World Cup games played in Seattle, including the United States’ 4-1 loss to Belgium in the Round of 16.

It was a challenge, but one he’d grown to handle.

“When 2026 hit, it was in some ways the hardest thing I've ever done professionally,” Destin said. “Super Bowl, World Cup, covering the Mariners, covering the Kraken, covering (University of Washington) football. But I got myself into a place (where) I can not only handle all this, but I can thrive and show up and be the best version of me, and that's super rewarding.”

Destin joined The Athletic, the New York Times’s sports department, in August 2026. He remains in Seattle as a Seahawks reporter and has been pleased with his time there so far.

“It’s forward-thinking, it’s progressive,” Destin said of The Athletic. “It’s, ‘Let's try different things, let's be creative, let's try and do the best work we possibly can.’ And I love that. I absolutely love that.”

Covering the Super Bowl would be a career-defining assignment for any journalist. So would a byline from the World Cup. At just 27 years old, Destin has both under his belt. And as far as he’s concerned, he’s not slowing down anytime soon.

“I'm very adamant, and I probably overdo it to some extent, but you should do things that make you happy as frequently as you possibly can, because at the end of the day, we're not going to be here forever,” Destin said. “That means hug your parents when you see them. Give it your all every time you go to the gym. Everything should be max effort. When you stop doing things (with) max effort in life, that's when you know you need to reevaluate.”

title: Penn State women’s volleyball set for ranked matches with No. 10 Oregon, No. 18 Indiana
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
After a trip to Los Angeles last week, No. 16 Penn State will step back into action this weekend.

The Nittany Lions were upset by UCLA in five sets before bouncing back with a sweep of USC. In the loss to the Bruins, outside hitters Kennedy Martin and Whitney Lauenstein led the blue and white with 25 and 19 kills, respectively.

The duo tacked on a combined 18 more in the three-set win over the Trojans to help rebound from the defeat.

“Kennedy at times can just take over a match,” coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley said at her weekly press conference. “She wants the ball all the time, and wants to find ways to score, and I think we've leaned on her for quite a few matches to score points for us, and I know she wants to do that, so we're not afraid to give her a lot of balls.”

Penn State now sits at 13-5 on the year and 5-3 in Big Ten play. The upset dropped the Nittany Lions a spot in the ranking after being No. 15 the week before.

On Friday, No. 10 Oregon will travel east to State College to take part in Penn State’s Dig Pink match, an annual event that is used to recognize survivors of breast cancer and raise funds to support breast cancer awareness.

The Ducks are 16-2 on the year, with their only losses coming in road matches against No. 7 Arizona State and No. 6 Wisconsin.

Since its last loss to the Badgers on Sept. 24, Oregon has beaten No. 15 Minnesota, No. 10 Purdue, No. 22 Michigan State and No. 18 Indiana.

The Ducks rank No. 7 nationally in kills per set, averaging 14.19. Sjakkie Donkers is responsible for many of them, averaging 3.78. Alanah Clemente and Valentina Vaulet also average more than three kills per set.

Defensively, Iva Sucurovic and Dalia Virlan lead the Ducks with 0.95 and 0.93 blocks per set, respectively.

Penn State is 6-3 all-time against Oregon and has won the last three matches between the teams dating back to 2022. Last season, the Nittany Lions beat the Ducks in a four-set victory in Eugene.

Friday’s first serve is set for 7 p.m., and the match can be streamed on Big Ten Plus.

“Every weekend in the Big Ten is tough, but I think this is a great opportunity to play two really great teams and two teams that are playing really well right now,” Schumacher-Cawley said at weekly media. “ I think Oregon, they've come a long way and they've gotten better every match they've played in. … it's nice to have them at home and use these days to prepare for not only Oregon but a really, really great IU team.”

With a quick turnaround, Penn State will fly to Bloomington Saturday for its matchup with Indiana the next day. The Hoosiers are slated No. 18 in the latest AVCA poll, unchanged from its last ranking. They’re 11-6 overall and an even 4-4 in conference play.

Indiana has played seven ranked opponents and taken down two, defeating No. 12 Texas A&M and sweeping No. 20 Washington.

Jaidyn Jager is the Hoosiers’ deadliest offensive threat, averaging 3.74 kills per set so far this season. Ella Boersema leads the team in hitting percentage at .337.

On defense, Indiana ranks last in the Big Ten with 11.37 digs per set, which is good news for the high-powered outside hitters that Penn State has on its roster.

The blue and white will also be without its key defensive anchor, middle blocker Ryla Jones, as Penn State Schumacher-Cawley confirmed at her weekly media that the junior will travel with the team to Bloomington but won't suit up yet.

There’s one word that can be used to describe the all-time series between Penn State and Indiana: dominant. The Nittany Lions hold a 62-2 record over the Hoosiers in a series that dates back to 1982.

Penn State was undefeated against the Hoosiers until 2010, when Indiana beat the Nittany Lions in four sets. The blue and white began another streak to follow, and didn’t drop a match until they were swept by the Hoosiers last season.

Sunday’s match is set for 3 p.m. and will be nationally televised on FS1.

title: Column | The good thing about being the first Penn Stater
author: Kippi Hall | The Daily Collegian
description:
I don’t come from a Penn State family. I didn’t wear a Nittany Lion onesie when I was a baby, nor did I have a favorite Berkey Creamery ice cream flavor before 2023. I first stepped foot onto campus when I was 16 years old, an experience hallmarked by my marveling at the view of Mount Nittany from campus and how many people they could cram onto College Avenue on a Friday night.

My family mostly went to the University of Pennsylvania with smatterings of Temple, Villanova and Widener. Newspaper clippings of a winning football team don’t line the walls of my house like a museum, and tailgating was reserved for the parking lots outside Lincoln Financial Field and Citizens Bank Park.

When I see the legacy Penn Staters posting old photos of current students at the Nittany Lion shrine as kids or donning “Party Like It’s 1986” T-shirts on gamedays, I always wonder what it must be like to get into Penn State with alumni down the hall. Is it a huge honor and a rite of passage, like coming home after a long trip? Are Family Weekends constant barrages of trips down memory lane and disappointment at how The Rathskeller isn’t there anymore?

My experience with Penn State is lined with discovery rather than nostalgia.

My oldest brother was the first in my family to go to Penn State. From there, my family and I made the three-and-a-half hour drive to State College, learning first hand about the Berkey Creamery, the Arboretum and that free public parking was a dream left over the mountains in Philadelphia.

When I got to campus, everything was still new and disorienting. Instead of a familiar homecoming like so many of my peers had, I was thrown into an unknown, isolated valley where mountain ridges replaced skyscrapers. The proud (and rightfully so) group of freshmen carrying the proverbial Penn State torch from their kin of alumni made me wonder if there was something I was missing by being a part of the first turn of the cycle in my family.

I remember walking down Bigler Road for the Homecoming Parade barely two months into freshman year, posing the surreal thought that the young faces watching the parade were at the same level of knowledge about the university as I was.

After four years as a student here, I think having a pair of fresh eyes to look at Happy Valley is one of the best things about going to Penn State before anyone else, and I was incredibly lucky to have the feeling of wonder contrasting those who were already used to the charm of State College from infancy.

Coming here with no expectations and no clue what a “grilled stickie” was allowed me to find some magic behind the borders of 16802. Despite how I love being a subway stop or two away from Center City, looking up at Mount Nittany instead of the Comcast Building still gives me a sense of majesty that’s hard to replicate with anything else. After 12 years in a gargantuan school district and a city where multiple colleges call home, having a solid identity in a town built around Penn State is wildly unique. The sore throat following a White Out game spent raising the decibel level to that of a jet engine taking off is worth it for a kind of hype I can’t find at home.

Even the little things that fade into the background for lifelong Penn Staters stand out to me. A fun fact I learned from my prior 18 years as a Philadelphian then living in Porter Hall: the Pollock residence halls are named exactly like streets in South Philadelphia, with duos of halls being named in the same order as neighboring streets.

I’m not deluded about where my original home is, and I would never shirk it from my identity. I still hear my family’s college stories from Smokey Joe’s – the UPenn equivalent to Doggie’s Pub, as far as I’m concerned – and I was rooting for the Quakers in March Madness before they were brutally defeated 105-70 by the Fighting Illini this year. Don’t worry, I made multiple brackets.

While I may have grown up giving a toast to dear old Penn, there’s no doubt in my mind I was meant to be at Dear Old State and I love being able to look at Penn State with a new lens.

As much as the outspoken families of Nittany Lions roar louder than the new kids on the block and provide a constant, needed loyalty to State, I hope the same wonder about Happy Valley shapes legacy students, too.

title: Penn State women’s soccer travels to Michigan to face the Spartans and Wolverine
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is heading into its last three matches of the regular season. After a 1-0 win over the Rutgers Scarlet Knights, the Nittany Lions now face a tough two-game road trip. They will head to Michigan to face off against the No. 5 Spartans and the No. 24 Wolverines on Thursday and Sunday, respectively.

Here's what you need to know.

Michigan State

The Spartans are coming off a 2-0 win against the Indiana Hoosiers. They are currently ranked fifth in the IWSOC poll and 3rd in the Big Ten standings and 6-1-1 at home this season.

Penn State coach Erica Dambach spoke with the media on Tuesday about the upcoming games and had this to say about the Spartans.

“What they do is what they do and they do it really well,” Dambach said. “It’s not a team that’s necessarily full of surprises; it’s a team that’s full of really experienced, talented players.”

The leaders of that experienced, talented team rank high in some Big Ten categories. Leading the team in points, senior forward Kennedy Bell has eight goals and eight assists this year. The Charlotte, North Carolina, native ranks fifth in shots on goal, second in assists, fourth in goals and third in points.

Not far behind Bell and right up there in the Big Ten rankings is senior midfielder Kayla Briggs. Briggs leads the team in assists with nine and is tied second in goals with six. The Toronto, Ontario native also ranked first in the conference in assists, third in game-winning goals, and fourth in points.

Michigan State has split goalkeeping duties almost 50/50, with Noelle Henning having eight starts and Bella Schopp seven, with each having only one loss this year. The better of the two is sophomore Henning with 24 saves and only four goals allowed.

The Milton, Ontario native ranks second in the Big Ten in goals-against average, third in saves, and seventh in shutouts per game.

Dambach said there's evidence to show her team can beat any team in the country.

“I want us to play that way. I want us to carry ourselves that way,” Dambach. “I want us to have the mentality from minute one to minute 90 that this is a team that can beat anyone in the country, regardless of what the number is before their name.”

Michigan

The Wolverines are coming off a 2-0 win against Oregon and will face off against the Maryland Terrapins on Thursday before playing the Nittany Lions. Michigan is currently ranked 24th in the country and seventh in the Big Ten, one spot behind Penn State.

Speaking to the media, Dambach said she and her team were focused only on the opponent in front of them.

“I don’t know anything about Michigan, in full transparency,” Dambach said. “Thursday’s a big one.”

What we do know about the Wolverines is that their leader in points is junior forward Ella Jablinskey, who has 18 points with eight goals and two assists on the year. The St. Clair native ranks tied third in goals in the conference, sixth in points and seventh in shots on goal.

The Wolverines’ second-best offensive weapon is senior midfielder Lilley Bosley, who ranks second on the team in points and goals and leads the team in assists. The Rochester, Michigan native also has two game-winning goals on the season.

Inside the box for Michigan is freshman keeper Mailia Zillman. The Waunakee, Wisconsin native has 50 saves to 16 goals allowed. Zillman also ranks eighth in the Big Ten in saves per game.

“I think that they’ve been very focused,” Dambach said. “They’ve been very intentional … just staying right here in the moment, staying off social media, staying off all of it, just win the games. You win the games, we’ll be fine.”

title: Preview | No. 19 Penn State field hockey hits the road for 2 ranked Big Ten matchups
author: Annie Gleba | The Daily Collegian
description:
Nittany Lions’ field hockey is officially ranked and primed to defend its post.

Penn State will play its last away games of the season against two ranked Big Ten teams. The Nittany Lions will face tough competition against No. 13 Indiana and No. 6 Iowa.

The blue and white enter this game ranked higher overall in Big Ten Play at No. 3 but lower in NFHCA rankings at No. 19. Coming out of this weekend with wins could help secure a top spot in the Big Ten tournament for the Nittany Lions.

Before this weekend’s games, Penn State has an overall record of 10-4 and 4-1 in conference play, with its only Big Ten loss coming to No. 1 Maryland. They have managed to keep up a seven-game win streak and have a record of 4-1 away.

Indiana

Indiana comes into this game with a 9-4 overall record and is tied with Penn State in conference play at 4-1. At home, they have been able to keep up a 4-1 record and have been able to beat two ranked opponents, Iowa and Michigan.

In Big Ten play, the Hoosiers have lost to No. 2 Northwestern and No. 6 Iowa when they played the Hawkeyes in a split weekend at Iowa City. That weekend showed that Indiana has dominated top teams in the past, being able to take the first win over Iowa 3-1, and just falling short 1-2 when the second game went to triple overtime.

The Indiana team has been able to showcase their tough offense by taking wins over ranked teams, but not falling short in a tough matchup. The team has scored a collective 34 goals this season and has an average of 2.62 goals per game.

The Hoosiers have two top offensive players, Molly Stutte and Celia Arroyo Cabezudo. Stutte has a total of 23 points and a breakout 42 shots on the season so far. The sophomore ranks No. 6 in shots and No. 9 in goals overall in the Big Ten.

Arroyo Cabezudo is another sophomore who has collected 20 points and 30 shots. She has a shots-on-goal percentage of 0.667 and has started and played through each game this season. Arroyo Cabezudo ranks No. 13 in shots and No. 10 in goals for the Big Ten.

Their main goalkeeper is Sadie Canelli; she has played in 12 games and started 11 of them, playing a total of just under 715 minutes. She has 38 saves and has a save percentage of 0.792, only allowing 10 goals this season.

In net for the Nittany Lions, the reliable Aby Deverka will continue to start and play the full game. She has amassed 54 saves, posting a 0.750 save percentage and allowing 18 goals this season. The Junior has climbed to No. 2 in saves per game among Big Ten goalies.

The two Big Ten teams will meet at 3 p.m. Friday.

Iowa

No. 6 Iowa sits at an overall record of 11-2 with a conference record of 3-2. The Hawkeyes have taken Big Ten losses to No. 13 Indiana and former No. 1 Northwestern. They have been able to defend their goal when at home and are 5-1 in Iowa City.

Iowa has developed a powerhouse offense, with players in the top of the Big Ten polls and a spread of players who have collected a significant number of points. Dionne van Aalsum, Frederique van Cleef, Felicia Zonnenberg, and Lieve van Kessel have topped the charts for the Hawkeyes.

Combined, they have a total of 120 points and 48 goals, but the player leading them is Van Aalsum, who has contributed 59 points and 28 goals. The Senior is the No. 1 player in the Big Ten for shots, game-winning goals, and shots on goal. The Nittany Lions will have to be on the lookout to cover the midfielder, not giving her opportunities to reach the circle if they want to keep goals and shots low.

Another Iowa player who is heavily ranked is Van Cleef; she is No. 1 in average goals per game and average points per game in the Big Ten. She is a 5th-year leader on the Hawkeyes and another key piece of their offense.

Flipping to Penn State’s offense, the Nittany Lion standouts continue to be Ella Gaitan, Oliva Martins, Sienna Dunn and Natalie Freeman. Gaitan leads the line with 24 points and 11 goals; she tops the Big Ten rankings at No.2 in shots and game-winning goals. Following her, Dunn leads the Big Ten in assists per game in the Big Ten. The duo will have to work together consistently this weekend to get past two top teams.

Penn State's last road game of the regular season will take place at noon and will feature Iowa’s Senior Day.

title: Penn State men's soccer has its work cut out for them against No. 18 Wisconsin this Saturday
author: Sienna Pearce | For The Collegian
description:
The Penn State Nittany Lions and Wisconsin Badgers will face off this Saturday at 7 pm in Jeffery Field in Happy Valley.

This game will be far from happy, though, as the Nittany Lions will be fighting to win over the Badgers, which they haven’t been able to do in past years. During the 2025 matchup, Penn State failed to get anything going and suffered a 2-0 loss. It will have to pull out all the stops to have a fighting chance this week.

This will be the 42nd time the two teams have played each other. Out of all of its meetings, Penn State has a 23-14-4 record.

Penn State’s season so far

This season, the Nittany Lions are 2-8-2. They haven’t had much luck against Big Ten opponents such as Washington, Michigan State, Indiana, UCLA and Ohio State.

Penn State has also been on an odd streak lately, tying its game against Michigan, finishing in a scoreless draw and a 1-1 game against Northwestern.

In their most recent game on Tuesday night, the Nittany Lions were crushed by the Rutgers Scarlet Knights, losing 5-0.

Penn State started the game off on the wrong foot after it failed to stop forward Dan Karsten from scoring Rutgers’ first goal in less than a minute.

“You give up a goal that early in the game, from a momentum standpoint, like in any sport, it sets the tone for the match,” Penn State coach Rob Dow said postgame after Rutgers. “We need to start games better; we need to respond to adversity better.”

The game continued to progress less than smoothly as forward striker Amadou Kone, defender Sheridan McNish and midfielder Dylan Carlson all earned yellow cards for unsportsmanlike behavior.

All hope was lost when the Scarlet Knights earned a 5-0 lead at the hour mark.

“I'm to blame for getting the team prepared for the game,” Dow said. “Collecting around the room to make sure that we're ready for matches and we're spotting diversity better.”

In goal for Penn State has been freshman Daniel Peluffo-Wiese, who’s played all but five minutes for the blue and white this season in net. Wiese posted a 2.17 goals against average with 37 saves and a disappointing 0.587 save percentage.

The 6-foot-7 netminder has notched two shutouts this season, but only one resulted in a win.

Wisconsin’s season so far

The Badgers enter Happy Valley at 9-2-3 this season. They have beaten notable Big Ten teams recently, such as defeating UCLA and Rutgers by one goal each.

Additionally, Wisconsin has tied against teams such as Washington (0-0), Indiana (1-1) and Ohio State (1-1).

In their most recent game Tuesday night, the Wisconsin Badgers earned a 2-1 victory over the Evansville Aces, scoring the game-winning goal in the last minute.

Midfielder Matthew Zachemski took the penalty kick awarded to Wisconsin and slammed it into the net, sealing its victory.

Netminder Judewellin Michel has seen most of the action in front of net for Wisconsin so far this season, starting in 13 of 14 potential games. The 6-foot-5 goalkeeper posted a 0.93 goals against average so far this season, with 36 shots for a 0.750 save percentage. The sophomore has also posted five shutouts this year.

title: Students participate in 'Walk a Mile in Her Shoes,' raise awareness for sexual assault, domestic violence
author: Curtis Johnson | For the Collegian
description:
Content warning: This article contains mention of sexual assault. Resources and support are available through Penn State’s Counseling and Psychological Services.

More than 100 Penn State students gathered for the “Walk a Mile in Her Shoes” march hosted by Voices Against Violence at the Allen Street Gates on Tuesday night. Participants, particularly men, were encouraged to walk a mile in high heels to raise awareness of sexual violence perpetuated against women.

Vice president and co-founder of Voices Against Violence, Carrisa Fan, 21, of Gilbert, Arizona, was initially drawn to the march because of its unconventional nature.

“I felt this was a very good way to get people turning their heads. You don’t see it in State College, Pennsylvania… multiple guys walking down the street in high heels,” Fan, a fourth-year studying nursing, said.

Fan and other organizers sought to balance the lighthearted nature of the march while maintaining the seriousness of sexual and domestic violence.

“People are not always going to come to an event if it’s not something that they think is fun,” Fan said.

However, she emphasized to all participants that “we were uncomfortable for 40 minutes, but people who were sexually assaulted in the past or have been in a domestically violent relationship will be uncomfortable for the rest of their life.”

Before the march began at 5:30 p.m., students created signs with messages such as “Abuse Has NO Excuse” and “Break the Silence, End the Violence!” Participants also wore purple ribbons in recognition of Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Nick Shriner, 18, of Arlington, Virginia, created a sign saying “No Means No!” and hoped the event could raise awareness about the experiences of sexual violence survivors to outsiders.

“Especially in light of recent events, we need to reinforce, like my sign says, that no means no and consent is always mandatory,” Shriner, a first-year studying agribusiness management, said.

The march began with cheers as participants waved their signs and started their mile-long walk in heels. Some participants who were unfamiliar with heels stumbled or even fell. As the march continued, onlookers cheered while passing cars honked their horns in support.

Connor Hoey, 20, of Carroll County, Maryland, described his first experience in heels as “definitely a calf workout” but said he hoped demonstrations such as these could spark conversations about sexual and domestic violence.

“Don’t be a bystander. If someone seeks out for help, help them,” Hoey, a second-year studying supply chain management and information systems, said.

Aiden Shepro, 20, of York, Pennsylvania, said he felt fraternities have to play an important role in organizing against domestic and sexual violence, particularly in light of recent sexual assault allegations at Cornell University. When Shepro, president of the Theta Chi fraternity at Penn State, received an email from Voices Against Violence about collaborating, he said he and his fraternity brothers were eager to participate.

“When can we go and do I need my own heels? There were just questions of how to get immediately involved,” Shepro, a third-year studying microbiology, said.

Shepro said participating in the march motivated him to take a more “proactive” role in preventing and ending sexual violence.

Other collaborating student organizations included the University Park Undergraduate Association (UPUA), which assisted with event planning, Serve State, which provided volunteers and Penn State Reproductive Justice Project, which provided first-aid assistance.

Beyond the march, Fan said she hoped Penn State would take additional steps to educate students about sexual and domestic violence.

“I’ve seen the emails… I just simply don’t think that’s enough. For most people, it goes to their spam,” Fan said. “I would love for people to have a course on campus that’s required by the school where they talk about statistics and resources that they do have.”

Fan encouraged survivors of sexual and domestic violence to seek assistance from the Relationship Violence Outreach, Intervention and Community Education (R-VOICE) Center at Penn State or the National Domestic Violence Hotline to reach help.

Looking ahead, Fan said she hopes that the success of the Walk a Mile in Her Shoes march will help establish the demonstration as an annual Penn State tradition every October.

“Don’t let the conversation die out now that the event is over,” Fan said.

Resources

Medical services include Mount Nittany Medical Center; Penn Highlands State College; and University Health Services.

On-campus resources include Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS); the Office of Sexual Misconduct Reporting & Response; the Relationship Violence Outreach, Intervention, and Community Education (R-VOICE) Center; and The Center for Sexual and Gender Diversity (CSGD).

Off-campus resources include Centre Safe.

title: Penn State men's soccer struggles without captain Joe Sheridan in blowout loss to Rutgers
author: Sawyer Klasnick | For The Collegian
description:
Last Friday night against Northwestern, sophomore Joe Sheridan delivered what might be the highlight of Penn State’s season by scoring the game-tying goal in the 81st minute.

However, just under ten minutes later, Sheridan received a red card after an apparent verbal altercation, which disqualified him for the rest of the game and Tuesday night's game against Rutgers.

Sheridan’s absence proved costly, as the Scarlet Knights blew out Penn State 5-0.

First-year coach Rob Dow mentioned the loss of his center back captain as part of the reason Penn State’s defense suffered Tuesday.

“We missed his leadership, his intensity, his reliability,” Dow said. “That’s 80 to 90% every single game, and he doesn't waver from that. You hear him up in the crowd trying to keep the guys motivated. He’s a top class player and a top class leader.”

The final score was indicative of the play on the field, as Rutgers outshot the Nittany Lions 19-6 and had 11 shots on goal to Penn State’s three.

With Sheridan sidelined, Dow had to rely on Noah Förster and freshman Sheridan McNish at center back. The Penn State coach was not impressed with what he saw.

“I saw a lot of first balls lost,” Dow said. “I saw a lot of times on the ball responding to the pressure they were getting on us, so it was like a snowball effect where we lost composure based on the pressure from direct play of Rutgers. We needed to see much more composure out of Noah, especially Noah here. He's a little bit older and has more experience. Sheridan's getting his first season in college, and has got a tremendous trajectory.”

The 6-foot-6 Sheridan was second on the team in points and minutes played entering Tuesday’s contest. He is also a team captain and Dow said he showed his leadership following his untimely red card.

“Yeah, he owned that,” Dowe said. “It was the first thing he did before the team trained in return from Northwestern. That's something he regrets.”

The lone Penn State player ahead of Sheridan in scoring, Amadou Kone, also didn’t start Tuesday’s match. However, it was not because of an injury or suspension.

“I think some other guys have performed better in the last two games, and so we got them off the bench a little more hungry, and you know that was the decision,” Dow said.

Kone, a senior from Ottawa, Canada, received a yellow card for unsporting behavior in the 42nd minute after entering the match. The inability to keep emotions in check was a theme for the Nittany Lions all night. After Rutgers forward Dan Karsten scored just 58 seconds into the match, Penn State was on its heels for the remainder of the night.

“Same thing, composure,” Dow said. “Next play mentality. But I'll be the first person, and so is the rest of the coaching staff, to be in the boat here, about getting beat. And I'm to blame for getting the team prepared for the game.”

Despite still being winless in Big Ten play, Dow knows what it takes to coach a winning team. During his time as the head coach at Vermont, Dow won the 2024 NCAA national championship. This season, as difficult as it has been, hasn’t discouraged him from believing that Penn State can reach those same heights.

“This team has worked too hard to not get a win,” Dow said. “You know, to get wins in the league. And personally, we're developing this team long term. And these are the days we'll look back in one year, two years, and have that channel in our mind that these are difficult but important lessons. We will learn from them.”

title: Penn State men’s hockey battles mentality struggles amid loss to Robert Morris, winless start
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
In the past two seasons, the Penn State program has seen new heights — its first-ever trip to the Frozen Four, acquiring the top prospect in college hockey and propelling itself into the spotlight as a national championship contender.

This season, however, the Nittany Lions have fallen to a 0-4 start, looking far off from the team that made history just last March.

The blue and white’s struggles continued Tuesday night with a 5-2 loss to Robert Morris, and head coach Guy Gadowsky pointed to the team’s mentality as a key factor.

“Very disappointed in the result, and very disappointed on how it happened,” Gadowsky said. “I’m just telling the honest truth about how I feel. I feel its arrogance. I feel that we feel we’re above what we had to do in the past to get where we got.”

The blue and white were fighting an uphill battle when, just 20 seconds in, defenseman Jackson Smith’s slapshot was blocked by Colonials captain Patrick Johnson, leading to a breakaway which Johnson finished with a shot that beat freshman goaltender Ryder Fetterolf on his blocker side.

Smith made another costly turnover which led to a 3-on-1 opportunity for Robert Morris, and junior forward Michael Felsing tapped it in on the doorstep with about four minutes to play in the first period.

“Jackson Smith is a great player,” Gadowsky said. “When he plays great, we’re a much better team.”

The Colonials added one more to their lead with just under 30 seconds to play in the first period. After Penn State was called for its fourth penalty of the period, senior forward George Krotiris buried a loose rebound and sent the home team into the locker room down three scores.

After 20 minutes, the Nittany Lions were heavily outplayed by a non-conference opponent that had also yet to win a game. They were outshot 15-6, and chasing a three-goal deficit that was fueled by self-inflicted wounds.

“I think it's just being more consistent, not letting a bad play affect how you react on the bench, and not letting a bad play affect your next shift,” captain Dane Dowiak said. “I think it's just coming out with the mentality that everybody's got to be pulling the rope the same way, and we haven't been doing that.”

Sophomore forward Justin Poirier cut into Robert Morris’ lead late in the second period with a backhand shot that got the blue and white on the board and breathed some life back into Pegula Ice Arena.

Poirier’s goal proved to be the only score of the middle frame, however, and Penn State continued to struggle with turnovers, failed zone entries, and difficulty gaining any sustained momentum.

“We're going to have to find a different way to prepare the team because it's not preparing them the same way,” Gadowsky said. “It was not getting the mentality results, and to me, that's what happened, and it's extremely disappointing.”

The final 20 minutes were much of the same struggles for the Nittany Lions.

Poirier pulled the blue and white within a goal after firing a shot from the left faceoff dot off the crossbar and in about five minutes in for his second of the game.

Penn State continued to get caught on its heels, however, and Krotiris also tallied his second of the night — this time giving Robert Morris back its two-goal lead — after going coast-to-coast and breezing past multiple defenders before tucking the puck behind Fetterolf.

An empty-net goal from Robert Morris’ Jackson Reineke sealed the Nittany Lions’ fourth straight loss, 5-2.

“It's unacceptable, being 0-4. That's not what we do here. I take full responsibility,” Dowiak said. “That's on me. I got to prepare the group better. But I'm confident we'll turn this thing around.”
